meta.title: AXT Inc. — Morris Young's InP and GaAs substrates through the 800G/1.6T photonics and CPO substrate inflection
meta.abstract: AXT, Inc. (NASDAQ: AXTI) is a Fremont, California-headquartered (US corporate) compound semiconductor substrate manufacturer operating principal production at its Beijing Tongmei (Tongmei) subsidiary in China. The company produces single-crystal indium phosphide (InP), gallium arsenide (GaAs), and germanium (Ge) substrates that serve as the foundational wafer material for compound semiconductor device manufacturing — InP for telecom/datacom laser diodes (800G/1.6T pluggable transceivers, coherent optics, CPO external light sources, silicon photonics flip-chip integration), GaAs for VCSELs (3D sensing, datacom), RF power (5G/6G base stations, military), and LEDs, and Ge for solar cells and broader specialty applications. Strategic narrative through 2024-2026 centers on (a) Tongmei STAR Market IPO pathway (long-awaited Shanghai STAR listing), (b) InP substrate demand inflection driven by 800G and emerging 1.6T datacom transceiver ramps plus the CPO architecture transition, (c) Chinese rare-earth and gallium/germanium export-control policy backdrop (Beijing's 2023-2024 gallium and germanium export controls cut both ways — restrictive on exports but supportive of Chinese-domiciled production), and (d) the multi-decade founder-led franchise narrative under CEO Morris Young.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
## One Layer Back From the Light

Somewhere between the raw crystal and the finished laser chip lies AXT, Inc. — and in the current build-out of AI data-centre optics, that position has become unusually valuable. As POET Technologies assembles its optical interposer and SIVERS Semiconductors fabricates its laser dice for high-speed transceivers, AXT supplies the single-crystal substrate from which those chips are grown: the compound semiconductor wafer that sets the electrical and optical properties of everything above it. Listed on NASDAQ as AXTI and headquartered in Fremont, California, with principal manufacturing through its Beijing Tongmei subsidiary in China, AXT is the upstream pure-play — structurally exposed to every 800G and 1.6T pluggable design-in and every co-packaged optics architecture shift, irrespective of which device-layer vendor ultimately prevails. The market cap is a fraction of the photonics names it feeds, yet the substrate demand accrues from the entire ecosystem's growth.

Dr. Morris S. Young co-founded the company in 1986 as American Xtal Technology and has served as chairman, president, and chief executive continuously since — one of the longest founder-CEO tenures in US-listed semiconductor history. Manufacturing migrated from Fremont to Beijing over the 2000s and 2010s, a transition that delivered cost-structure advantages and deep vertical integration into raw materials. Tongmei subsidiaries — Baoding Tongmei, Nanjing Jinmei, JinMei, and Chaoyang Tongmei — produce the high-purity gallium, arsenic, germanium, and pyrolytic boron nitride crucibles consumed in the internal crystal-growth flow.

## Three Substrate Chemistries

AXT's portfolio organises around three compound semiconductor families. Indium phosphide (InP), grown across 2-inch through 6-inch diameters, is the telecom and datacom laser substrate: the crystalline platform for the EML, DFB, and tunable laser diodes that drive 100G through 1.6T optical transceivers, coherent modules, and the external light source units at the heart of co-packaged optics architectures. Gallium arsenide (GaAs), in both semi-insulating and semi-conducting variants, serves VCSELs in Apple Face ID and automotive LiDAR, RF power amplifiers for 5G and 6G infrastructure, and related optoelectronic devices. Germanium (Ge) substrates address multi-junction solar cells for space applications and infrared optics — smaller revenue but strategically adjacent to defence-adjacent supply chains.

InP is the current thesis driver. In the first quarter of 2026, InP substrates generated $13.6 million of AXT's $26.9 million consolidated revenue — crossing a majority share for the first time — alongside GaAs at $5.4 million, germanium at $0.2 million, and raw-material joint-venture sales at $7.6 million. [Q1 2026 earnings call, Motley Fool transcript](https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/04/30/axt-axti-q1-2026-earnings-call-transcript/)

## The 2025 Trough: Export Permits and Margin Compression

Fiscal 2025 was defined by regulatory friction, not demand. Full-year revenue was $88.3 million, an 11% decline from $99.4 million in fiscal 2024. GAAP gross margin compressed to 12.7% from 24.0%, and the GAAP net loss nearly doubled, from $11.6 million in 2024 to $21.3 million in 2025, or $0.49 per diluted share. The damage concentrated in the first half: Q1 and Q2 2025 produced only $19.4 million and $18.0 million respectively. China's gallium and germanium export controls, in force since August 2023, were progressively tightened — extended to additional strategic materials in December 2024 and, from 4 February 2025, explicitly applied to InP substrates, each shipment now requiring individual authorisation from Beijing authorities. CFO Gary Fischer described the permit regime as "not predictable, nor in our control."

The controls cut bilaterally. They disrupted AXT's ability to serve US and European customers on schedule, with US tariffs on Chinese-manufactured wafers simultaneously rising to 70%, compressing North American revenue from approximately 8% of total in 2024 to roughly 2% in 2025. In the opposite direction, they reinforced the structural moat of a Beijing-domiciled supplier with captive gallium, arsenide, and indium phosphide feedstock access — reducing the practical ability of European or Japanese competitors to replicate the integrated supply chain. [Stocktitan AXTI 2025 10-K analysis](https://www.stocktitan.net/sec-filings/AXTI/10-k-axt-inc-files-annual-report-ed35d0270da0.html)

## The Inflection and the Backlog

Q3 2025 signalled the turn. InP revenues grew more than 250% sequentially and reached a three-year high. By the Q1 2026 earnings call in late April, the InP order backlog had climbed to what Young called "a new high of over $100 million," with COO Tim Bettles noting the company was "qualifying and supplying wafers to a lot of new tier-one customers in this field." Young stated flatly: "We believe that today our material is being used in multiple U.S. hyperscalers." Q1 2026 GAAP gross margin recovered to 29.6%, and Q2 2026 guidance pointed to approximately $34 million in realisable revenue — the company's anticipated return to profitability — with non-GAAP EPS guided to $0.06–$0.08. [MarketBeat Q1 2026 earnings call highlights](https://www.marketbeat.com/instant-alerts/axt-q1-earnings-call-highlights-2026-04-30/)

AXT is racing capacity to match the backlog. The roadmap targets $35 million of quarterly InP output by year-end 2026, roughly doubling from early-2026 run rates, and $65 million to $70 million per quarter by 2027–2028. CPO external light source volumes represent, in Young's phrasing, "another inflection point in our business beginning in late 2027 and beyond."

## Tongmei IPO and the Dossier's Questions

The Tongmei STAR Market IPO remains the structural wildcard. Beijing Tongmei submitted its Shanghai Stock Exchange application in January 2022; the SSE approved the listing in July 2022 and the CSRC accepted the filing for review in August 2022. As of Q1 2026, approval had not been granted. Fischer noted Tongmei "remains in process as a part of a much more selective and smaller group of prospective listings" — narrowed, not withdrawn. A completed offering would unlock minority-interest value at the subsidiary level and provide capital for the capacity expansion now running ahead of schedule.

This dossier examines AXT along five structural axes: whether InP capacity can be scaled in time to convert a $100 million backlog into revenue at pace; the degree of customer concentration at the substrate layer where a single device-maker can redirect allocation; the capital-structure and governance implications of a Tongmei listing; the geopolitical framework for a US-headquartered company whose entire manufacturing perimeter sits inside China's export-control regime; and competitive positioning against Sumitomo Electric of Japan, Freiberger Compound Materials of Germany, and Wafer Technology of the United Kingdom in a substrate market Young projects will grow four to six times within three to five years.

> "The market for optical components will increase significantly in the coming years, driving a four to six times increase in the substrate market overall in the next three to five years." — Morris Young, Q1 2026 earnings call

chapters.title: From 1986 American Xtal founding through Beijing Tongmei migration to the Tongmei STAR IPO pursuit
chapters.body:
## Fremont, 1986: Morris Young and the VGF Breakthrough

The company that became AXT, Inc. traces its origin to 1986, when Morris Young incorporated American Xtal Technology in Fremont, California, a city already threading itself into the emerging electronics supply chain of Silicon Valley's outer orbit. Young, a materials scientist with deep expertise in compound semiconductors, founded the enterprise around a proprietary crystal-growth technique he believed could reshape the economics of the substrate business: vertical gradient freeze, or VGF.

The dominant method at the time for producing gallium arsenide substrates was liquid encapsulated Czochralski — LEC — a high-temperature crystal-pulling process that generated elevated dislocation densities in the resulting boule. VGF worked differently: the technique grew crystal by slowly advancing a controlled thermal gradient upward through a vertical furnace configuration, allowing the semiconductor crystal to solidify from the bottom under substantially lower thermal stress. The result was substrates with significantly lower etch pit density, a quality metric that mattered acutely to the laser diode and high-frequency electronic device manufacturers who were American Xtal Technology's earliest target customers.

VGF was not Young's invention alone — Japanese and European researchers had explored gradient-freeze variants for decades — but Young and his Fremont team developed a commercially scalable implementation that could produce semi-insulating and semi-conducting GaAs substrates to the tight specifications demanded by device makers. By the early 1990s, American Xtal Technology had established itself as a credible alternative to the Japanese and German substrate incumbents that dominated global supply. The company listed on the NASDAQ Stock Market as AXT, Inc. and broadened its substrate portfolio beyond GaAs to include indium phosphide for telecom laser diode applications and germanium for multi-junction space solar cells — two product lines that would, three decades later, form the strategic core of the company's demand thesis around 800G datacom and Co-Packaged Optics architectures.

Young has remained Founder, Chairman, President, and Chief Executive Officer without interruption since 1986, making his tenure among the longest unbroken founder-CEO runs in the US-listed compound semiconductor universe.

## The Beijing Migration: Manufacturing Logic of the 2000s

The most consequential structural decision in AXT's history was not made at founding but during the 2000s: the phased transfer of principal manufacturing from Fremont to a dedicated subsidiary in Beijing. Beijing Tongmei Xtal Technology Co., Ltd. — referred to throughout the company's SEC filings simply as "Beijing Tongmei" or "Tongmei" — became the operational engine of the enterprise, eventually housing the bulk of AXT's VGF crystal-growth furnaces, polishing lines, and wafer-finishing capacity.

The strategic logic was direct. Compound semiconductor substrate manufacturing is labour-intensive at the polishing and lapping stages, energy-intensive at the crystal-growth stage, and critically dependent on proximity to high-purity raw-material inputs — principally gallium, arsenic, phosphorus, indium, and germanium. China offered lower labour costs, competitive industrial energy pricing, and geographic proximity to the domestic sources of those inputs. Manufacturing in Beijing did not merely lower the cost of existing production volumes; it made capacity expansions economically viable that would have been prohibitive in California at equivalent utilisation economics.

The migration also carried a second-order strategic logic that would not become apparent to outside observers for more than a decade. By anchoring its manufacturing within China's industrial ecosystem rather than supplying it from offshore, AXT embedded itself as a participant in the Chinese compound semiconductor supply chain. That positioning — an American-headquartered, NASDAQ-listed parent with its principal operating subsidiary incorporated and operating inside China — would acquire outsized significance when Beijing began asserting export-control authority over gallium and germanium raw materials in 2023.

By the conclusion of the migration period, Fremont retained a lean US corporate, sales, and investor-relations function. Beijing Tongmei housed the operating engine. The revenue base flowed principally through substrate shipments from Tongmei to external device manufacturers across Japan, Europe, China, and North America.

## Vertical Integration: Controlling the Supply Chain

AXT's most underappreciated structural asset is not the substrate business itself but the cluster of upstream raw-material subsidiaries assembled to control the inputs to crystal growth. The vertical integration architecture spans multiple Chinese entities, each focused on a specific material in the compound semiconductor production flow.

Baoding Tongmei supplies high-purity gallium, the principal raw material for GaAs substrates and a co-input for indium phosphide. Nanjing Jinmei and the JinMei entity address high-purity arsenic and adjacent materials. Chaoyang Tongmei contributes additional upstream raw-material capacity. Together, the cluster forms an internal supply chain that insulates AXT's substrate manufacturing from spot-market pricing volatility and availability risk — a structural advantage over non-integrated competitors who must source high-purity gallium and germanium from external refiners.

The integration extends to a further specialty input: pyrolytic boron nitride, or pBN, the high-purity crucible material in which VGF crystal growth occurs. pBN crucibles are consumed during the crystal-growth process and represent a recurring cost centre for any substrate manufacturer. AXT's control of pBN crucible production within its own subsidiary network provides a cost and operational stability advantage that compounds across high-volume production cycles.

The strategic value of this upstream architecture became acutely visible in August 2023, when Beijing imposed export licencing requirements on all gallium and germanium shipments leaving China. The controls — effective immediately upon announcement — created supply-chain anxiety for compound semiconductor manufacturers globally, and produced a sharp rally in gallium and germanium spot prices as buyers outside China scrambled to assess exposure. For AXT, the controls cut in both directions. The licencing requirements created new frictions in the movement of raw materials and substrates across Chinese borders. But they simultaneously reinforced the competitive value of AXT's Chinese-domiciled, vertically integrated manufacturing position — a configuration that rivals based solely in Japan, Germany, or the United Kingdom could not replicate quickly, if at all.

## The Tongmei STAR Market Pursuit: 2021 Onward

Beginning in 2021, AXT initiated a formal process to list Beijing Tongmei on the STAR Market of the Shanghai Stock Exchange — China's technology-focused growth board, established in 2019 and modelled in part on the NASDAQ listing framework. A successful Tongmei IPO would allow AXT to monetise a minority stake in its Chinese operating core, raise capital to fund InP and GaAs capacity expansion, and establish a Tongmei equity valuation independent of the US-listed parent.

The process advanced through the review apparatus of the China Securities Regulatory Commission and the Shanghai Stock Exchange across multiple calendar years. STAR Market applications require completion of a multi-round comment-letter process in which regulators scrutinise financials, related-party transaction disclosure, governance structures, and the applicant's credentials as a science and technology enterprise — a classification threshold central to STAR Market eligibility. For Tongmei, a compound semiconductor substrate manufacturer with deep linkages to AXT's US-listed parent and an upstream raw-material subsidiary network, each of those dimensions required careful structuring and disclosure.

The review calendar stretched through 2021, 2022, and 2023 without resolution, reflecting both the complexity of the Tongmei filing and the broader CSRC pipeline dynamics during a period of episodic regulatory tightening across China's IPO market. By 2024 and into 2025, the Tongmei STAR Market listing remained pending, with management acknowledging the timeline uncertainty on successive earnings calls while reaffirming the company's commitment to completion. The IPO's resolution, management has noted repeatedly, is substantially a function of Chinese regulatory scheduling rather than AXT corporate will.

The strategic significance of a completed listing extends well beyond the immediate capital raise. A STAR Market Tongmei would carry the credibility of onshore Chinese exchange disclosure, differentiating it from foreign-controlled substrate suppliers at a moment when Chinese industrial policy increasingly favours domestic sourcing across the semiconductor supply chain. It would also establish a Beijing Tongmei equity currency for potential future partnerships or acquisitions within China's compound semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem. The Tongmei IPO has thus functioned for nearly five years as the central re-rating catalyst in the AXT investment thesis — a prospective unlock whose timing, as of the frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026, remained open.

chapters.title: InP, GaAs, Ge substrates and the compound semiconductor substrate value chain
chapters.body:
## Atoms of Light: The Three-Family Substrate Portfolio

The compound semiconductor substrate sits at a peculiarly leveraged position in the photonics supply chain. AXT, Inc. — operating principally through its Beijing Tongmei manufacturing subsidiary — sold single-crystal wafers of indium phosphide, gallium arsenide, and germanium to the device makers who sliced, polished, and epitaxially grew the laser chips, VCSELs, and transistor structures that powered the world's optical networks, smartphones, and military electronics. AXT's customers were one processing step closer to the device than AXT itself. That positioning meant the company captured neither the headline value of a finished laser chip nor the brand recognition of the transceiver module in the faceplate of a rack switch — but it did capture the structural demand signal of every photonics architecture cycle, arriving slightly upstream and therefore slightly earlier than its customers' own volume ramps.

## Indium Phosphide: The Core Photonics Substrate

Of the three substrate families, indium phosphide carried the highest strategic weight by the mid-2020s. InP is the material of choice for DFB (distributed feedback) lasers, EML (electro-absorption modulated laser) chips, tunable laser sources, and coherent modulators — the core light-emitting elements in optical transceivers from 100G through the 400G, 800G, and emerging 1.6T generations. The compound's direct bandgap and electron mobility characteristics made it essentially irreplaceable for high-speed telecom and datacom laser applications; silicon photonics platforms needed InP-based light sources precisely because silicon could not efficiently emit light.

AXT manufactured InP substrates across four principal wafer diameters: two-inch, three-inch, four-inch, and six-inch. The diameter progression tracked the industry's ongoing push toward higher throughput per reactor run — larger substrates meant more laser bars per MOCVD epitaxial growth cycle, compressing device cost. The transition toward four-inch and six-inch InP was the manufacturing conversation of the early 2020s: six-inch InP substrates had been commercially rare, and achieving the crystalline quality and surface uniformity needed for high-volume DFB and EML production at that diameter required years of crystal growth process refinement.

Doping variants expanded the addressable application set. Iron (Fe)-doped, semi-insulating InP substrates served applications demanding low electrical conductivity beneath the device layer — coherent modulator structures and certain high-frequency photonic integrated circuit architectures. Sulfur (S)-doped, n-type conducting substrates addressed the bulk of DFB and EML laser production. Undoped, semi-insulating variants served research applications and some quantum photonics work. The multiplicity of specifications created process complexity that favored incumbent substrate manufacturers with established quality-control infrastructure.

The demand inflection that defined AXT's positioning through 2024 and 2025 was structural rather than cyclical. Hyperscaler data-center operators — chasing the bandwidth density demanded by large-scale AI training and inference clusters — drove a generational transceiver upgrade from 400G to 800G pluggable modules, and engineering development for 1.6T pluggable and co-packaged optics (CPO) architectures was well advanced within the frozen window. Every 800G transceiver required DFB or EML laser chips grown on InP substrates. Every external light source module for a CPO implementation — whether a multi-wavelength laser array flip-chip integrated onto a silicon photonics platform or a discrete chip attached to a silicon waveguide — traced its optical power back to an InP wafer.

The CPO architecture introduced a structural thesis for InP substrate volumes that differed qualitatively from the pluggable transceiver market. Where pluggable transceivers numbered in the millions of units annually across the industry, a CPO external light source module could require a higher InP area per port at scale, and the architectural shift from pluggable to embedded optics in switch ASICs was projected to reach production volumes in the 2026–2028 window — meaningfully beyond the frozen window but within the planning horizon that shaped AXTI's capacity investment decisions. Morris Young, speaking in earnings calls through this period, described InP as the substrate family where demand visibility had most improved.

## Gallium Arsenide: VCSELs, RF, and the Apple Effect

Gallium arsenide substrates served a more heterogeneous application set. AXT produced both semi-insulating (SI) and semi-conducting (SC) variants, and the distinction mattered commercially. Semi-insulating GaAs provided the high-resistivity, trap-free substrate platform on which compound semiconductor foundries grew HBT (heterojunction bipolar transistor) and PHEMT (pseudomorphic high-electron-mobility transistor) device structures for 5G and 6G RF front-end modules, military radar, and power amplifier applications. Customers in this segment included RF power semiconductor makers supplying the base-station and handset markets. Semi-conducting GaAs substrates served VCSEL (vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser) production, LED manufacturing, and laser diode applications for industrial and consumer markets.

VCSEL demand had been shaped, unusually visibly, by a single consumer product: the Apple iPhone Face ID system. Apple's adoption of VCSEL-based structured-light 3D sensing for facial recognition beginning in 2017 pulled the entire GaAs substrate supply chain toward capacity expansion and quality improvement. VCSEL array production for Face ID used semi-conducting GaAs substrates grown to strict uniformity specifications, and the volume requirements from Apple's annual iPhone refresh cycle created a demand pulse that reverberated upstream to AXT. Automotive LiDAR extended the VCSEL substrate thesis into a second market — depth-sensing lidar stacks for advanced driver-assistance systems required VCSEL arrays at power densities and beam qualities that similarly demanded high-specification GaAs substrates. Datacom VCSEL applications — short-reach multimode fiber links inside data centers — added a third demand pillar.

By the mid-2020s, GaAs substrate demand was maturing relative to InP's inflection trajectory. The VCSEL 3D sensing market had developed a more predictable demand cadence as smartphone penetration of the technology stabilized, and the incremental demand signal came from automotive LiDAR volume ramps and the datacom VCSEL market. The RF GaAs substrate market tracked the 5G infrastructure buildout and handset content expansion.

## Germanium: Space and Terrestrial Solar

Germanium substrates served a narrower, higher-margin niche. Multi-junction solar cells for space applications — satellite power systems, deep-space probes — used germanium as the substrate for monolithic Ge/GaAs/InGaP triple-junction structures, leveraging germanium's lattice constant compatibility with the III-V compound layers grown above. Space solar cell production was a low-volume, high-specification market where substrate quality translated directly to satellite mission reliability, and customers such as Spectrolab (a Boeing subsidiary) and Azur Space in Germany represented the principal demand sources. Concentrated photovoltaic (CPV) systems for terrestrial solar energy applications constituted a secondary market, though CPV's commercial trajectory had proven more difficult than early projections suggested. Infrared optics applications — germanium's transparency in the mid-infrared spectrum made it useful for thermal imaging lenses and windows — added further diversification to the Ge substrate franchise.

## VGF Crystal Growth and the Process Foundation

AXT built its substrate manufacturing franchise on the vertical gradient freeze (VGF) crystal growth process. VGF — in which a compound semiconductor melt is directionally solidified from bottom to top inside a sealed ampoule, with a controlled temperature gradient moving slowly upward — produced single-crystal boules with lower dislocation densities than competing Czochralski or horizontal Bridgman methods for InP and GaAs. Lower etch pit density (EPD) in the finished substrate translated to higher yields in downstream epitaxial growth and device fabrication, making VGF-grown wafers the preferred platform for demanding DFB laser and VCSEL applications. The pyrolytic boron nitride (pBN) crucibles used to contain the melt during VGF growth were manufactured internally through Chaoyang Tongmei, the company's pBN subsidiary — a materials-quality and supply-chain-control advantage that competitors sourcing crucibles from third parties did not share.

## Upstream Vertical Integration: The Raw-Material Subsidiaries

AXT's vertical integration extended well upstream of the crystal growth step. Baoding Tongmei produced high-purity gallium — the principal precursor for both GaAs and, in combination with arsenic, part of the broader compound semiconductor feedstock ecosystem. Nanjing Jinmei and JinMei contributed additional high-purity materials production capacity. Chaoyang Tongmei, as noted, supplied pBN crucibles. This integration gave AXT cost-structure visibility and supply security advantages that a purely substrate-focused manufacturer purchasing all raw materials on the open market would have lacked.

The strategic salience of this integration sharpened materially in August 2023, when China's Ministry of Commerce announced export controls on gallium and germanium products — a retaliatory measure in the broader semiconductor technology competition with the United States and its allies. The controls cut ambivalently for AXT: restrictions on raw-material exports from China affected the broader supply chain, but AXT's Chinese-domiciled substrate manufacturing operations and Chinese-domiciled raw-material subsidiaries meant the company was largely operating within the regulated supply envelope rather than across it. AXT sold substrates from Beijing Tongmei into the global compound semiconductor device market; the export-control regime created friction for competitors sourcing Chinese gallium or germanium from arm's-length suppliers while AXT's internal supply flow remained operationally coherent, though not entirely free of regulatory scrutiny and compliance overhead.

## Competitive Positioning in the Substrate Tier

| Substrate Family | Principal AXT Competitor(s) | AXT Competitive Basis |
|---|---|---|
| InP | Sumitomo Electric (Japan), Wafer Technology (UK) | VGF crystal quality, 4"/6" diameter scaling, vertical raw-material integration |
| GaAs (SI/SC) | Freiberger Compound Materials (Germany), Sumitomo Electric, Wafer Technology | VGF EPD performance, VCSEL-grade SC wafer uniformity, cost structure |
| Ge | Umicore (Belgium) | Vertical Ge feedstock integration, established space-solar qualification |

Sumitomo Electric represented the most technically formidable InP competitor, with deep process experience and established relationships with Japanese photonics customers. Freiberger's GaAs franchise was oriented more heavily toward European and North American RF and VCSEL customers. Wafer Technology served research and smaller-volume production markets. AXT's competitive differentiation rested on the combination of VGF process discipline, pBN crucible control, upstream raw-material integration, and the scale of the Beijing Tongmei manufacturing facility — a compound of advantages that any single-dimension competitor could not easily replicate. The substrate market's appetite for supplier qualification discipline — device makers invested heavily in qualifying a substrate vendor and changed slowly — further reinforced AXT's installed customer base across all three product families.

chapters.title: Revenue trajectory, substrate ASPs, Tongmei IPO unlock, capital structure
chapters.body:
The financial architecture of AXT, Inc. is inseparable from the cyclicality of compound semiconductor demand. Revenue oscillated through a wide band across the four fiscal years spanning 2022 to 2025, swinging from a cyclical peak driven by the VCSEL 3D sensing wave and accelerating InP datacom adoption, through a sharp correction as the compound semiconductor inventory cycle turned, and then recovering on the back of a structural demand inflection in indium phosphide substrates driven by 800G and emerging 1.6T optical transceiver architectures. Against that backdrop, two longer-running threads — the pursuit of a Beijing Tongmei STAR Market IPO and the vertical integration advantage crystallised by China's 2023 gallium and germanium export controls — shaped the capital structure and cost dynamics in ways that will define AXT's financial profile through the decade.

## Revenue Trajectory: Peak, Correction, and InP-Led Recovery

AXT entered 2022 at the tail end of a VCSEL-driven boom. Fiscal 2021 had been a record revenue year for the Fremont-headquartered substrate maker, with demand from Apple's Face ID supply chain, automotive LiDAR programmes, and broadening InP datacom deployments running simultaneously. In fiscal 2022, the company reported revenue of approximately $143 million — still near peak levels, per the [AXTI FY2022 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=AXTI&type=10-K&dateb=&owner=include&count=40) — though the year carried an important internal inflection: GaAs substrate demand, particularly from VCSEL customers, began softening in the second half as consumer electronics OEMs worked through elevated inventories, while InP continued to advance on the strength of 400G coherent module ramps and early 800G transceiver qualification at Lumentum, Coherent, and the major Japanese photonics houses.

The correction arrived with force in 2023. Full-year revenue fell to approximately $100 million as disclosed in the [AXTI FY2023 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=AXTI&type=10-K&dateb=&owner=include&count=40), a decline of roughly thirty percent from the prior peak. The GaAs substrate business bore the sharpest contraction: VCSEL demand from 3D sensing applications thinned as smartphone unit volume softened globally and Apple managed its supply chain inventories aggressively. RF power GaAs remained more resilient — 5G infrastructure spending continued, though at a more measured pace — but could not offset the VCSEL-related customer drawdowns. Germanium substrates held approximately steady in dollar contribution, their multi-junction solar cell customer base substantially insulated from consumer electronics cycles.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (approx.) | Key Driver | Trend |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | ~$143M | GaAs VCSEL peak; InP 400G ramp | Peak/plateau |
| FY2023 | ~$100M | GaAs/VCSEL correction; InP resilient | Sharp decline |
| FY2024 | Recovery | InP 800G inflection; GaAs stabilising | Rebound |
| FY2025 | Continued recovery | InP 800G + 1.6T; CPO thesis building | Expansion |

*Sources: AXTI FY2022 and FY2023 10-K filings; FY2024–2025 from sequential 10-Q disclosures and earnings call commentary.*

Recovery took shape through 2024. The InP substrate business, which had remained the most structurally resilient segment through the correction, accelerated as hyperscaler data-centre operators began deploying 800G optical transceiver infrastructure at scale. InP-based directly modulated lasers, electro-absorption modulated lasers, and tunable coherent sources all required incremental substrate supply, and AXT was among a small number of commercially qualified InP substrate suppliers globally. Quarterly revenue at AXT moved progressively higher through 2024, with the company disclosing improving InP order visibility in successive 10-Q filings. The emerging co-packaged optics thesis — which envisions InP-based external light source modules integrated directly alongside ASIC packages — added structural credibility to the multi-year InP demand narrative entering 2025.

## Substrate ASP Architecture: The InP Premium

The substrate mix story is primarily an average selling price story. InP single-crystal wafers command substantially higher ASPs than GaAs substrates of equivalent diameter, reflecting the more demanding crystal-growth chemistry — liquid-encapsulated Czochralski for InP versus vertical gradient freeze for GaAs — the smaller addressable supply base, and tighter end-application specifications around surface quality, dislocation density, and carrier concentration uniformity. At 4-inch and 6-inch diameters, the InP ASP premium over GaAs is material at the unit level; AXT's blended revenue-per-wafer trends in annual filings confirm that periods of higher InP mix carry disproportionately higher revenue relative to wafer-count volume.

GaAs substrates, lower in ASP per wafer, constitute the majority of unit volume and contribute the largest single dollar block to revenue at cycle peaks. The substrate comes in semi-insulating form for VCSEL and photonic devices and semi-conducting form for solar cell and LED applications. The mix between research-grade and production-grade wafers, and between smaller two-inch and three-inch formats versus larger-diameter six-inch wafers, shifts the blended GaAs ASP within any quarter. AXT has consistently indicated that the transition toward larger-diameter wafers carries a pricing premium and yields operating leverage through higher throughput per crystal-growth run — a structural argument for margin expansion as the six-inch GaAs transition matures.

Germanium substrates occupy a speciality niche. Revenues are modest in absolute terms but carry attractive margin characteristics, underpinned by captive upstream supply of high-purity germanium through the Chaoyang Tongmei and Nanjing Jinmei raw-material subsidiaries. The space multi-junction solar cell market, served through customers including Spectrolab and Azur Space, is a relatively steady buyer even through compound semiconductor cycles, providing a low-volatility revenue floor beneath the more cyclical InP and GaAs businesses.

## Gross Margin Mechanics and Operating Leverage

AXT's gross margin is acutely sensitive to capacity utilisation at Beijing Tongmei's crystal-growth operations, which carry a meaningful fixed cost base — furnace capital, facility overhead, and a core technical workforce that cannot be scaled down proportionately with volume. When revenue compresses toward or through $100 million, as it did during the 2023 trough, gross margins thin toward breakeven on an operating basis, and the company's SEC filings through that period disclosed negative or near-zero operating income. The dynamic is symmetrical in recovery. As InP and GaAs volumes increase against a relatively stable fixed cost base, incremental gross margin on each additional revenue dollar runs substantially above the reported average — a leverage profile that makes AXT's profitability trajectory highly convex to the substrate demand cycle.

Management commentary across multiple earnings calls framed the mechanics directly, noting that InP's higher ASP means each incremental InP wafer shipped carries outsized gross margin contribution relative to the consolidated average, and that returning the Beijing Tongmei facility to higher utilisation levels was the primary lever for restoring operating profitability. Selling, general, and administrative costs have been held relatively flat, consistent with AXT's lean US corporate structure in Fremont and a manufacturing-centred cost base in Beijing. Research and development expenditure remains modest as a percentage of revenue, reflecting AXT's positioning as a volume substrate manufacturer rather than a device-level technology developer.

## The Tongmei STAR Market IPO: Timeline and Capital Structure Implications

No strategic item occupied more investor attention across the 2022–2025 period than the pending STAR Market Shanghai IPO of Beijing Tongmei Xtal Technology Co., Ltd. — the Chinese manufacturing subsidiary that houses AXT's substrate production and, through its affiliate network, its raw-material sourcing operations.

AXT initiated the Tongmei STAR Market listing process in 2021, filing the requisite application to the China Securities Regulatory Commission under the registration-based IPO framework that the STAR Market pioneered. The rationale was unambiguous: a domestic Chinese listing would furnish Tongmei with renminbi-denominated capital to fund capacity expansion — incremental crystal-growth furnaces, larger-diameter wafer polishing lines, and upstream raw-material processing infrastructure — while crystallising the value of AXT's majority stake and potentially extending Tongmei's commercial credibility with Chinese compound semiconductor customers whose strategic importance was growing as China's domestic optical device industry scaled.

The CSRC review process proved extended. Multiple rounds of regulatory inquiry — standard under the STAR Market's science-and-technology disclosure requirements — pushed timelines well past initial estimates. AXT's annual reports and 8-K filings through 2022 and 2023 acknowledged the ongoing CSRC review process without committing to specific closure dates. The broader pause in Chinese IPO activity through 2022–2023, as Beijing moderated equity market activity amid macro pressures, added an external headwind to Tongmei's listing timeline.

The capital structure implications of a completed IPO are substantial. AXT holds a majority interest in Tongmei; minority shareholders, including Tongmei employees and pre-IPO investors, hold the remainder. A STAR Market listing would create a publicly traded price discovery mechanism for the manufacturing subsidiary, effectively disaggregating the value of AXT's Chinese operations from the consolidated AXTI market capitalisation. On the consolidated AXT balance sheet, the non-controlling interest line — representing the minority's economic claim on Tongmei's net assets — would reset to fair market value at IPO pricing rather than the historical cost basis carried under the current accounting treatment. The accounting reclassification alone would represent a meaningful change to reported equity and minority-interest dynamics, quite apart from the operational capital inflows.

The gallium and germanium export controls imposed by China in August 2023 added a dual-use dimension to the Tongmei IPO calculus: a domestically listed, STAR Market-registered entity may navigate China's evolving strategic-mineral regulatory regime with somewhat smoother institutional framing than a wholly-owned subsidiary of a US-listed parent. As of the frozen snapshot date of May 2026, the Tongmei STAR Market IPO remained an open but unresolved event — still capable of delivering a step-change in AXT's capital structure and providing the funding base for the next phase of InP and GaAs capacity buildout.

## Cash Position, Working Capital, and the Raw-Material Subsidiary Contribution

AXT has historically maintained a conservative balance sheet. Cash and cash equivalents, together with short-term investments, have provided a liquidity buffer through the substrate cycle — supporting the company through the 2023 trough without recourse to material external financing. The company's SEC filings disclosed cash balances typically in the $30–60 million range across recent periods, with working capital dynamics shaped significantly by inventory levels. During the 2023 correction, raw-material and work-in-process inventories needed active management as production volumes fell — a dynamic that consumed cash and depressed near-term cash generation even as the company maintained positive liquidity.

The raw-material subsidiaries — Baoding Tongmei producing high-purity gallium and arsenic, Nanjing Jinmei and JinMei supplying high-purity germanium, and Chaoyang Tongmei contributing additional germanium and specialty materials — contribute to AXT's consolidated financial profile primarily through intercompany transfer pricing rather than as stand-alone external revenue generators. By supplying precursor materials to Beijing Tongmei at internally determined prices, these entities provide AXT with both cost visibility and margin capture that a pure substrate assembler relying on spot-market raw-material procurement would lack entirely.

The August 2023 China gallium export controls — which imposed licensing requirements for gallium exports outside China — validated the strategic value of this vertical integration in terms the financial statements could not fully capture. While the controls constrained the theoretical market for selling Chinese-sourced gallium externally, they secured AXT's internal supply chain against the tighter spot-market pricing that emerged as non-Chinese buyers scrambled to diversify gallium sourcing. The simultaneous germanium controls carried analogous implications for AXT's Ge substrate cost base. The consolidated financial picture entering 2026 was therefore one of operating recovery — revenues rebuilding on InP demand strength, gross margins expanding on operating leverage, a conservative balance sheet carrying adequate liquidity, and a potentially transformative IPO event still pending resolution.

chapters.title: Quarterly cadence through China export controls, photonics demand, and Tongmei IPO milestones
chapters.body:
## The Peak and the Reckoning, 2022

AXT entered 2022 riding a demand curve that had rewarded patience. Revenue had climbed to $137.4 million in fiscal 2021 and then reached $141.1 million in fiscal 2022, with gross margins expanding to 37.2 percent — the strongest profitability in the company's modern history. In the first quarter of that year, indium phosphide substrates alone generated $15.5 million in revenue, with gallium arsenide contributing $12.0 million and germanium $4.2 million out of a $39.7 million consolidated total. The substrate cycle was at high tide.

The turn came swiftly. Gallium arsenide, supplying wireless infrastructure, consumer headsets, and industrial lasers — applications concentrated in China — was the first to crack. By the fourth quarter of 2022, GaAs revenue had collapsed to $5.5 million, down 33 percent sequentially and 51 percent year-over-year, as Chinese OEM customers decelerated sharply into an inventory overhang. InP held longer: Q4 2022 InP revenue of $14.0 million was still 6.9 percent higher year-over-year, though down 26 percent from the prior quarter's $17.7 million as early destocking reached the telecom-datacom supply chain.

> "Gallium arsenide revenue is down significantly off its mid-2022 highs, with customers in China having slowed significantly." — Morris Young, Q4 2022 earnings call

The full weight of the correction hit in fiscal 2023. Annual revenue fell to $75.8 million — a 46 percent contraction from the prior year's peak — and GAAP gross margin collapsed to 17.6 percent. The company reported a net loss of $17.9 million, the largest in recent memory. Quarterly InP revenue, which had exceeded $15 million in each of the first two quarters of 2022, scraped along at $4.6 million in Q2 2023 and $4.9 million in Q3 2023 as the telecom-datacom inventory glut proved deeper and longer than management had initially anticipated. Ge substrate revenue, tied to multi-junction solar cells for satellites, added marginal ballast: $2.2 million in Q3 2023 before falling back to $1.1 million in Q4.

> "Gallium arsenide was the first of our materials to experience the micro-downturn, beginning in Q3 of last year. We actually already have seen two quarters of improvement, although very, very slight." — Morris Young, Q2 2023

---

## The Export-Control Inflection: August 2023

While the substrate cycle was still grinding toward its trough, a geopolitical event introduced a new structural variable. On July 3, 2023, Beijing announced that gallium and germanium — two elements central to AXT's raw-materials subsidiaries — would require export permits effective August 1. The announcement swept across the compound semiconductor industry. AXT's vertically integrated structure, with raw-material operations including JinMei (gallium) and Nanjing Jinmei embedded inside China, placed the company directly inside the regulatory perimeter.

Management moved quickly to characterise the exposure. On August 3, in the Q2 2023 call, Young said that JinMei's exports outside of China had comprised less than 2 percent of its Q2 sales and that no meaningful direct impact to consolidated revenue was expected. The assessment proved broadly accurate for the initial round: within six weeks, Tongmei had secured preliminary permits and resumed shipments of gallium arsenide and germanium substrates to a growing roster of customers.

> "In September Tongmei received initial export licenses and was able to resume shipping gallium arsenide substrates and germanium substrates to a number of our customers." — Morris Young, Q3 2023

CFO Gary Fischer noted that the permit process was iterative, customer-by-customer, with approvals taking weeks rather than days. The administrative friction was real but manageable. The deeper significance of August 2023 was not the immediate revenue disruption but the regulatory architecture it revealed: Beijing had asserted the right to license compound semiconductor exports across the full supply chain, a power that would prove far more consequential eighteen months later when the scope widened to include indium phosphide.

---

## Recovery and the AI Awakening, 2024

The cycle turned measurably in fiscal 2024. Consolidated revenue recovered to $99.4 million, a 31 percent rebound from the 2023 trough, and GAAP gross margin expanded to 24.0 percent. The proximate drivers were InP recovery in the first half and GaAs stabilisation throughout. In Q1 2024, total revenue of $22.7 million reflected InP growing 48 percent sequentially from the Q4 2023 base; Q2 2024 followed at $27.9 million, up 23 percent sequentially and 50 percent year-over-year. By that point, management's language had shifted from inventory-cycle commentary to genuine demand excitement.

> "We understand from our customers that our indium phosphide substrates are currently being utilized for high-speed optical components for artificial intelligence interconnects and we are working closely with a number of customers building next-generation lasers for use in data center transceivers." — Morris Young, Q1 2024

The signal was consistent across every subsequent quarter of 2024. In August, Young noted that adoption in "new applications, such as AI where we expect that indium phosphide will be required in optical transceivers for high-speed data transmission" was accelerating. By October, Q3 2024 results showed total revenue of $23.6 million — up 36 percent year-over-year — with management pointing out that every product line including raw materials had achieved double-digit year-over-year growth, the first such sweep since 2021. Q4 2024 closed the year at $25.1 million quarterly revenue, with InP at $9.1 million, GaAs recovering to $5.4 million, and raw materials at $9.0 million.

On the competitive front, management flagged meaningful GaAs share gains: AXT had grown its HBT market share from zero to approximately 10 percent and was targeting 30 percent. The recovery was broadening across substrate families.

The Tongmei STAR Market pursuit, meanwhile, was in its third year of regulatory review. The Shanghai Stock Exchange had formally accepted Tongmei's application in January 2022 and approved the listing in July 2022. The China Securities Regulatory Commission had accepted it for review in August 2022. By the 2024 annual filing, the process remained active, with management continuing to report it as in process. The contingent liability — a redemption obligation to the ten private-equity funds that had invested roughly $49 million for a 7.28 percent redeemable stake in January 2021 — remained disclosed in every 10-K. If the IPO were abandoned or rejected, AXT would be required to repurchase those shares at the original purchase price.

---

## The February 2025 Shock and the Permit Regime

On February 4, 2025, Beijing extended its compound semiconductor export-control regime to include indium phosphide. The move was not wholly unanticipated — AXT's 10-K risk disclosures had flagged the possibility — but the timing, arriving while the company was in the early stages of what management was describing as an AI-driven structural demand uplift, was severe. First-quarter 2025 InP revenue fell 58 percent quarter-over-quarter. Consolidated revenue dropped to $19.4 million, and GAAP gross margin turned negative for the first time in the company's modern history, reaching minus 6.4 percent. The net loss for the quarter was $8.8 million, or $0.20 per diluted share.

> "While the geopolitical environment is creating undeniable challenges, we are focusing our energies where we can drive positive returns today." — Morris Young, Q1 2025

The second quarter confirmed the permit regime's bite. Consolidated revenue declined further to $18.0 million, with InP falling to $3.6 million — restricted almost entirely to domestic Chinese customers purchasing for PON and local data-centre applications. The first export permit for InP shipments outside China was granted only in late June 2025, yielding approximately $700,000 in international InP revenue for the quarter. GAAP gross margin remained depressed at roughly 8 percent non-GAAP. Young told investors that "delays in Q2 resulted in our being able to ship less material outside of China than anticipated" and that the company was "taking a conservative view of the timing of larger permits in Q3."

The conservative guidance proved wrong in the most welcome direction. Third-quarter 2025 InP permits arrived in volume. Revenue surged to $28.0 million for the quarter — up 56 percent sequentially and 18 percent year-over-year, materially ahead of guidance of $19 to $21 million. InP alone reached $13.1 million, a 250 percent sequential increase and a three-year high. InP backlog climbed above $49 million.

> "This has been a highly active time for our business with the strong uptick in indium phosphide demand from data-center applications globally." — Morris Young, Q3 2025

The fourth quarter exposed the permit regime's volatility in the opposite direction. Despite a backlog that had not shrunk, permit approvals in Q4 2025 came in lighter than management expected, and InP revenue fell back to $8.0 million. Consolidated revenue was $23.0 million, with non-GAAP gross margin of 21.5 percent and a net loss of approximately $2.3 million. Young acknowledged being "disappointed that we didn't receive as many export permits in Q4 as we had hoped." The full fiscal year 2025 produced $88.3 million in revenue — below the 2024 recovery level — with GAAP gross margin of approximately 13 percent, a year defined less by demand than by regulatory friction.

---

## Q1 2026 and the Backlog Inflection

The most current data point within the frozen window is the first quarter of 2026, reported April 30, 2026. Revenue of $26.9 million reflected InP returning to $13.6 million — 50.6 percent of consolidated revenue — on the back of permits that had arrived with greater regularity than in Q4 2025. Non-GAAP gross margin of 29.9 percent was the highest since 2022. The net loss had narrowed to $0.59 million, or $0.01 per diluted share, with first GAAP profitability expected in Q2 2026 at guided revenue of approximately $34 million.

> "This is an incredibly exciting time for AXT…indium phosphide substrates are a key ingredient in high-speed optical data transmission required in AI focused data centers. The massive AI infrastructure build out…is the primary driver for EML and silicon photonics-based optical transceivers." — Morris Young, Q1 2026

InP backlog had surpassed $100 million — a record — driven by demand from EML chips, continuous-wave lasers for silicon photonics modules, and the emerging co-packaged optics ecosystem. Chinese InP-based laser revenue in China more than doubled in Q1, with further doubling expected in Q2. CFO Gary Fischer noted approximately $26 million in "realizable" revenue entering Q1 already covered by permits or not requiring them, with "potential significant upside from additional permits."

Alongside the quarterly results, AXT announced completion of a $632.5 million capital raise to fund Tongmei's InP capacity expansion and 6-inch InP wafer development — a figure that dwarfed the company's consolidated annual revenue and reflected the scale of demand that management was attempting to position against. On the Tongmei STAR Market IPO, Young and Fischer confirmed the process remained active, now in a "much more selective and smaller group of prospective listings" than at the time of original submission, with no abandonment and no updated timeline offered.

The arc from the 2022 revenue peak through the 2023 inventory correction, the August 2023 gallium and germanium export controls, the 2024 InP recovery, and the February 2025 InP export-control shock traces a company whose fundamental demand thesis — that indium phosphide substrates would become critical infrastructure for AI-era optical interconnects — had vindicated itself even as the regulatory and geopolitical environment imposed a stop-start cadence that no conventional supply-demand model had anticipated.

chapters.title: Morris Young, CFO, executive team, and the board
chapters.body:
When Morris Shen-Shin Young left AT&T Bell Laboratories for Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in the mid-1980s, the field of compound semiconductor crystal growth was still largely a province of defence contractors and national laboratories. Young had studied metallurgical engineering at Taiwan's National Cheng Kung University, then pursued advanced degrees in metallurgy at Syracuse University and Polytechnic University in Brooklyn, and the progression had made him unusually fluent in the materials science of III-V compounds — the binary alloys of group-III and group-V elements whose electronic and optical properties silicon could not replicate. In December 1986, he left Livermore to co-found American Xtal Technology in Fremont, California, a city that would remain the company's legal and administrative domicile for the next four decades. The company would eventually rename itself AXT, Inc. in July 2000 and complete an initial public offering on NASDAQ in 1998, but its founding logic had been set in that first year: manufacture the single-crystal substrate wafers that the rest of the compound semiconductor industry depended upon.

## A Founder Who Came Back

Young's tenure at the company he created has been long but not uninterrupted. He served as President and Chief Executive Officer from 1989 through May 2004 and simultaneously as Chairman of the Board from February 1998 through May 2004, guiding AXT through its California manufacturing years, its NASDAQ listing, and the initial migration of gallium arsenide production to Beijing in the early 2000s. In 2004 he stepped back from operational leadership, transitioning to Chief Technology Officer, and subsequently retired from the company in 2006.

The intervening years did not age AXT well. The company cycled through leadership changes and board restructurings, and in July 2009 the board reappointed Young as Chief Executive Officer — a return that has, by 2026, extended for more than fifteen years. The title of Chairman of the Board followed on 12 August 2021, consolidating the combined chairman-CEO structure that the company has maintained since. Young holds both roles concurrently as of the frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026, making him one of the longest-serving founder-CEOs in the US-listed compound semiconductor universe.

As reported in the company's most recent proxy filing, Young's base salary was increased from $479,000 to $518,000 per year effective November 2025, an 8.1 percent adjustment, with total reported compensation for fiscal 2025 reaching approximately $1,673,000 inclusive of stock-based components. His beneficial ownership — held substantially through the Young Family Trust and the Morris Young Family Limited Partnership — stood at roughly five million shares of AXT common stock, representing the largest single insider block in the register.

In AXT's earnings disclosures, Young's public statements have grown notably more pointed as the InP demand cycle has inflected. After AXT obtained Chinese export permits enabling resumption of indium phosphide shipments in the third quarter of 2025, he said:

> "This has been a highly active time for our business with the strong uptick in indium phosphide demand from data center applications globally. In Q3, our indium phosphide revenues grew more than 250 percent sequentially and reached a three-year high as we obtained export permits for a number of significant indium phosphide orders throughout the quarter."

Looking forward to 2026, he characterised the demand environment as:

> "With strong, ongoing market trends fueling the data center upgrade cycle, we believe we have tremendous opportunity in 2026 to drive meaningful growth in our business and a return to profitability."

## The Finance Function

The principal financial counterpart to Young is [Gary L. Fischer](https://investors.axt.com/Investors/governance/executive-management/default.aspx), who joined AXT in August 2014 as Vice President, Chief Financial Officer, and Corporate Secretary. Fischer brings a Silicon Valley career arc built on public-company finance: prior CFO postings at companies in the memory-solutions and GPS-technology sectors, experience taking companies through IPO processes, and a background in merger-and-acquisition execution. He holds an MBA from Santa Clara University and a bachelor's degree from the University of California, Santa Barbara.

By the time of the FY2025 proxy filing, Fischer was 74 years old and had held the AXT CFO title for more than a decade — an unusual durability in a role that typically sees higher turnover at small-cap technology companies. His base salary was raised from $354,000 to $385,000 per year effective November 2025, an 8.8 percent increase, and his disclosed beneficial ownership stood at approximately 362,000 shares. Beneath Fischer in the US financial organisation sits Alan Chan, Vice President of Finance and Corporate Controller, based in Fremont, who handles day-to-day accounting and reporting operations.

## Vincent Liu and the Tongmei Operation

The executive whose tenure most directly shaped the company's competitive position is neither Young nor Fischer but Vincent Liu, General Manager and Vice President of AXT China — the architect of the Beijing Tongmei operation. Liu joined American Xtal Technology in March 1993 as a manufacturing engineer and progressed through roles of increasing operational responsibility over the following decade. When AXT made the strategic decision to migrate its gallium arsenide crystal-growth manufacturing from Fremont to China, Liu led the China-side execution: site selection in Beijing, infrastructure build-out, technology transfer, and ultimately the establishment of Beijing Tongmei Xtal Technology Co., Ltd. as AXT's principal manufacturing subsidiary. Volume production of GaAs substrate wafers in Beijing commenced in 2000, and Liu has managed the Tongmei operation since its inception.

That tenure now exceeds three decades in total and twenty-five years as Tongmei's operating head. The subsidiary Liu oversees encompasses not only the Beijing crystal-growth facility but a vertically integrated network of raw-material subsidiaries — Baoding Tongmei, Nanjing Jinmei, JinMei, and Chaoyang Tongmei — that produce high-purity gallium, arsenic, and germanium feedstock and pyrolytic boron nitride crucibles for the internal manufacturing flow. Tongmei's long-pending STAR Market Shanghai IPO, pursued from 2021 onward through multiple regulatory review cycles, would if consummated represent a partial monetisation of the China operation that Liu built.

## The Board: Composition and Continuity

The AXT board entering 2026 comprised four members: Young as non-independent Chairman and CEO, and three independent directors — Jesse Chen, David C. Chang, and Leonard J. LeBlanc.

[Jesse Chen](https://investors.axt.com/Investors/governance/board-of-directors/default.aspx), Lead Independent Director and a board member since February 1998, has served the company across the longest arc of any outside director. He was CEO of BusLogic, Inc., a semiconductor and computer-peripherals company, from 1990 to 1996, and has served since 1997 as managing director of Maton Ventures. During the years of Young's retirement from operations, Chen served twice as non-executive Chairman — from May 2004 to October 2007 and again from March 2009 until Young's return to the chairmanship in August 2021. He holds a B.S. in aeronautical engineering from National Cheng Kung University in Taiwan and an M.S. in electrical engineering from Loyola Marymount University; as with Young and Chang, the NCKUT educational thread runs through the board, a reflection of the Taiwan-US engineering emigration wave of the 1970s and 1980s that seeded much of Silicon Valley's semiconductor industry. Chen chairs the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee.

[David C. Chang, Ph.D.](https://investors.axt.com/Investors/governance/board-of-directors/default.aspx), who joined the board in December 2000, brings an academic-scientific background unusual among directors of semiconductor companies. Chang earned a B.S. in electrical engineering from National Cheng Kung University, then an M.S. and Ph.D. in applied physics from Harvard University. He served as President of Polytechnic University from 1994 to 2005 — the same institution from which Young received his doctoral degree in metallurgy — and as Chancellor of the expanded NYU Polytechnic School of Engineering from 2005 to 2013, where he now holds the rank of Professor Emeritus. In 2011 he co-founded The Global Maximum Educational Opportunities and has served as its Chairman and Chief Executive Officer since 2013. He chairs the Compensation Committee. The overlap between Chang's academic home institution and Young's doctoral alma mater is not incidental; Polytechnic University was one of the few US institutions in the 1980s running serious programmes at the intersection of materials science and applied physics with relevance to III-V semiconductors.

[Leonard J. LeBlanc](https://www.stocktitan.net/sec-filings/AXTI/8-k-axt-inc-reports-material-event-5bcc0b858b2f.html) returned to the board in July 2025, filling the vacancy created by the passing of Christine Russell. LeBlanc had previously served as an AXT director from April 2003 to December 2021. His career is anchored in public-company finance: CFO tenures at Cadence Design Systems, Infoseek, Vantive, and Ebest, plus prior board service at Oplink Communications, which operated in the optical components space directly adjacent to AXT's customer base. He holds degrees from Holy Cross and a master's degree in finance from George Washington University. In January 2026 the board designated LeBlanc Chair of the Audit Committee and confirmed his independence under Nasdaq Listing Rules.

Christine Russell, who joined the board in December 2019 and had served as Audit Committee Chair, died in July 2025. During her tenure she brought active CFO-level semiconductor sector experience — including her role as CFO of PDF Solutions, Inc. and prior postings at EAG, Inc. and Virage Logic — that had strengthened the board's financial oversight of an operation whose principal manufacturing assets sit inside a Chinese subsidiary.

## Governance Architecture

The board maintains a combined Chairman-and-CEO structure, offset by the Lead Independent Director role held by Jesse Chen. All three independent directors satisfy the independence requirements of the Nasdaq Listing Rules; the Audit, Compensation, and Nominating/Corporate Governance committees are each composed exclusively of independent directors. A clawback policy covering incentive-based compensation was adopted on 8 November 2023 in compliance with SEC rules adopted under the Dodd-Frank Act. The company's insider-trading policy prohibits executives and directors from pledging or hedging AXT common stock. The May 2025 advisory say-on-pay vote recorded 88.4 percent approval, suggesting shareholders found the compensation structure broadly acceptable despite the company's protracted period of below-cost revenues through the gallium export-restriction cycle of 2023-2025.

| Director | Age (2025 proxy) | Director Since | Independence | Primary Committee Role |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Morris S. Young, Ph.D. | 81 | 1989 | Non-independent | Chairman / CEO |
| Jesse Chen | 68 | 1998 | Independent | Lead Independent; Nom/Gov Chair |
| David C. Chang, Ph.D. | 84 | 2000 | Independent | Compensation Chair |
| Leonard J. LeBlanc | 85 | 2025 (re-joined) | Independent | Audit Chair |

The compact board size — four members — reflects a deliberate governance choice at a company where the founder retains operational control and institutional shareholders are relatively limited. Young's combined role as Chairman, CEO, and President means that strategic direction, operational execution, and board agenda-setting converge in a single individual who has been present since the company's December 1986 California incorporation. The independent-director cohort, by contrast, skews older and longer-tenured than typical mid-cap technology boards, a configuration that prioritises continuity and founder-alignment over the periodic refreshment that proxy-advisory guidelines increasingly recommend.

---

*Sources: [AXT DEF 14A FY2025 — SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001051627/000155837025004393/axti-20250515xdef14a.htm); [AXT Board of Directors IR page](https://investors.axt.com/Investors/governance/board-of-directors/default.aspx); [AXT Executive Management IR page](https://investors.axt.com/Investors/governance/executive-management/default.aspx); [Christine Russell appointment press release](https://www.globenewswire.com/en/news-release/2020/01/07/1967574/0/en/Christine-Russell-Appointed-to-AXT-Inc.-Board-of-Directors.html); [AXT Q3 2025 results](https://investors.axt.com/Investors/news/news-details/2025/AXT-Inc--Announces-Third-Quarter-2025-Financial-Results/default.aspx); [StockTitan DEF 14A summary](https://www.stocktitan.net/sec-filings/AXTI/def-14a-axt-inc-definitive-proxy-statement-f4d623704a52.html); [LeBlanc board appointment 8-K](https://www.stocktitan.net/sec-filings/AXTI/8-k-axt-inc-reports-material-event-5bcc0b858b2f.html)*

chapters.title: Compound semiconductor device makers, VCSEL ecosystem, RF power, multi-junction solar
chapters.body:
## Epi-Wafer Foundries: IQE, Coherent, and the Substrate-to-Epitaxy Chain

AXT's substrate business sits one layer upstream from the active device, selling polished single-crystal wafers to customers who deposit thin-film epitaxial structures before fabricating laser diodes, VCSELs, photodetectors, or transistors. The most consequential link in that chain is the epi-wafer foundry segment, where IQE plc of Cardiff and the post-merger Coherent Corporation represent two distinct purchasing profiles.

IQE, the world's largest independent compound semiconductor epi-wafer supplier, grows III-V epitaxial layers on substrates sourced from multiple vendors. Its business spans VCSEL epi-wafers for consumer 3D sensing, photovoltaic epi for space solar, and RF epi for mobile front-end modules — making it a natural customer across AXT's InP, GaAs, and Ge portfolio. IQE's purchasing volumes track its own customer wins: a new smartphone VCSEL design win translates upstream into GaAs substrate demand that flows partly to AXT.

Coherent Corporation — assembled through the 2022 merger of II-VI Incorporated and legacy Coherent Corp, itself built on II-VI's prior acquisitions of Finisar and others — occupies a different structural position. Coherent is vertically integrated from substrate growth through chip fabrication to transceiver module assembly, but its InP and GaAs chip volumes are large enough that it sources substrates externally alongside internal crystal-growth capacity. As a buyer of InP substrates for telecom and datacom laser diodes and GaAs substrates for VCSEL and free-space optics applications, Coherent represents one of the more sizable addressable accounts in AXT's customer universe.

Lumentum Holdings rounds out the US-headquartered epi-to-device tier. A major supplier of pump lasers, DFB lasers, tunable lasers, and VCSELs, Lumentum's fabrication lines consume InP substrates for telecom-wavelength laser diodes and GaAs substrates for the VCSEL product family that includes the Apple Face ID emitter supply chain. Lumentum and II-VI were the two principal VCSEL suppliers to Apple for the TrueDepth 3D sensing module introduced with the iPhone X, a relationship that created a structurally elevated demand baseline for 6-inch GaAs semi-insulating substrates beginning in the late 2010s.

Sumitomo Electric Industries, the Japanese conglomerate with a compound photonics division spanning single-mode fiber, laser diodes, and photodetectors, is among the long-tenured Japanese optical component makers that purchase AXT substrates. Sumitomo Electric's optical devices unit fabricates DFB lasers and EML transmitters for optical transceivers, with InP substrate consumption tied closely to datacom transceiver ramp cycles.

## Japanese Photonics and the Chinese Optical Module Tier

The vertically integrated Japanese photonics segment — Mitsubishi Electric, Sharp, Sony, and their component subsidiaries — constitutes a durable demand base that predates the 800G inflection. Mitsubishi Electric's optical device division produces laser diodes and high-power semiconductor lasers across telecom and industrial applications. Sharp and Sony maintain compound photonics units addressing consumer and industrial markets, including laser diode arrays, infrared emitters, and optical pickups. These relationships are characterized by stability and long qualification cycles: once an AXT substrate is qualified into a Japanese OEM's laser diode production line, displacement requires a multi-year requalification process, giving AXT defensible repeat-purchase volumes.

The rise of Chinese optical module manufacturers created an additional demand vector, particularly for InP substrates as Chinese component makers scaled coherent transceiver capacity alongside the global 400G-to-800G transition. Accelink Technologies, the Wuhan-based optical component and module maker backed by Fiberhome Group, grew into one of China's most significant optical transceiver manufacturers. The broader cluster of Chinese optical module makers — servicing domestic hyperscaler builds as well as export sales to global data-center operators — was both a customer for AXT's InP substrates through Beijing Tongmei and a beneficiary of the same gallium and germanium export-control regime that periodically constrained raw-material flows outside China's borders.

## The VCSEL Ecosystem and Apple's Face ID Dependency

No single application drove more GaAs substrate unit demand in the 2017–2023 period than the VCSEL array used in Apple's Face ID TrueDepth camera system. Each iPhone fitted with Face ID requires a VCSEL array, a flood illuminator, and an infrared dot projector — all fabricated on GaAs substrates. Apple's annual iPhone volumes, typically north of 200 million units, created a structural consumption floor for 6-inch semi-insulating GaAs wafers. Lumentum and II-VI split the VCSEL supply position across successive iPhone generations, sourcing GaAs substrates from multiple vendors; AXT, as a principal supplier, benefited from the resulting demand step-up — though the consumer cycle also exposed the company to Apple's notoriously concentrated and variable component-sourcing calendar.

Beyond smartphones, the VCSEL market expanded into automotive LiDAR, datacom short-reach interconnects, and industrial sensing. ams OSRAM — formed through ams AG's 2020 acquisition of the OSRAM Opto Semiconductors business — is a significant VCSEL maker serving consumer and automotive 3D sensing markets. Trumpf, the German laser systems company, added VCSEL capabilities for industrial applications. The automotive LiDAR wave, driven by ADAS adoption across major vehicle platforms, introduced a qualitatively different demand profile: lower peak volumes than smartphones but multi-year production commitments and stringent AEC-Q101 qualification requirements that made substrate vendor switching costly.

The datacom VCSEL segment — 850 nm arrays for short-reach multimode fiber links inside hyperscaler data centers — added a third demand vector. While datacom VCSELs are lower-cost and higher-volume than LiDAR equivalents, they are directly exposed to the same hyperscaler capex cycle that drives InP demand, making GaAs and InP substrate consumption partially correlated to the same underlying data-center build-out through 2024–2025.

## RF Power: Qorvo, MACOM, and the 5G Infrastructure Cycle

GaAs substrates for RF applications address a structurally different segment of AXT's customer base. Qorvo — formed from the 2015 merger of RF Micro Devices and TriQuint Semiconductor — became the world's largest compound semiconductor RF component maker by revenue, manufacturing GaAs HBT power amplifiers for mobile handset front-end modules and GaN-on-SiC power amplifiers for base-station infrastructure. Its GaAs device fabs sourced semi-insulating substrates from multiple vendors including AXT.

MACOM Technology Solutions pursued a complementary strategy, serving infrastructure, defense, and data-center interconnect markets with GaAs, GaN, and InP devices. MACOM's InP photodetectors and transimpedance amplifiers for data-center optical receivers made it a dual-substrate customer — purchasing both GaAs for RF applications and InP for photonic integrated circuit components. The 5G base-station infrastructure cycle that accelerated from 2019 through 2023, particularly across China and in global markets, elevated GaAs substrate demand from both Qorvo and MACOM alongside the broader RF front-end module tier. The subsequent 6G research and early-development cycle, which intensified through 2024–2025, maintained RF compound semiconductor demand at elevated levels even as 5G handset unit volumes plateaued.

## Multi-Junction Solar: Spectrolab, Azur Space, and LEO Proliferation

The germanium substrate segment connected AXT to the most capital-intensive and geopolitically distinctive end-market in its portfolio: space. Multi-junction solar cells — three- or four-junction devices with efficiencies exceeding 30 percent — use germanium as the bottom junction and mechanical substrate. Ge wafers must be grown to tight specifications for lattice constant, carrier concentration, and surface finish, since defect densities propagate upward through the epitaxial junctions deposited on top.

Spectrolab, the Boeing subsidiary based in Sylmar, California, has been the principal supplier of multi-junction solar cells to US space programs since the 1990s, serving NASA, the Department of Defense, and commercial satellite operators. Azur Space Solar Power, based in Heilbronn, Germany, serves the European space supply chain with equivalent triple-junction and four-junction products. Both companies sourced Ge substrates from AXT and from Umicore's semiconductor division, the other principal Ge wafer supplier globally.

The proliferation of low-Earth orbit satellite constellations — SpaceX Starlink, Amazon Kuiper, Telesat Lightspeed, and national LEO programs — expanded annual Ge substrate consumption volumes beyond the traditional geostationary satellite cadence. LEO constellations require far greater numbers of satellites than traditional GEO birds, with shorter design lifetimes and planned replacement cycles, sustaining a higher annual launch rate and a correspondingly higher substrate demand floor through the mid-2020s.

| End-Market | Primary Substrate | Key Customers | Principal Demand Driver |
|---|---|---|---|
| Telecom/datacom laser diodes | InP | Coherent, Lumentum, Sumitomo Electric, Accelink | 800G/1.6T transceiver ramp; CPO external light source |
| VCSEL — 3D sensing | GaAs (SI) | Lumentum, Coherent, ams OSRAM | Apple Face ID; automotive LiDAR |
| VCSEL — datacom | GaAs (SI) | Coherent, Lumentum | Hyperscaler short-reach interconnect |
| RF power amplifiers | GaAs (SI) | Qorvo, MACOM | 5G/6G handset and base-station |
| Multi-junction solar | Ge | Spectrolab, Azur Space | LEO constellation build-out; GEO satellites |
| Epi-wafer foundry | InP, GaAs | IQE, Coherent | III-V device outsourcing |
