Across all five segments, the structural pattern was the same: AXT sat at the front of the compound semiconductor supply chain, selling a consumed material input that had to be qualified into each customer's production process and then reordered at volume as device production scaled. The combination of InP's 800G-driven momentum, GaAs's Apple-anchored VCSEL baseline, and Ge's LEO-fueled space demand created, by the mid-2020s, an unusually aligned multi-segment demand environment — one that the company's Beijing Tongmei manufacturing platform was positioned to serve from a single vertically integrated production complex, and one whose durability remained inseparable from the geopolitical and regulatory conditions surrounding that complex's continued operation.

chapters.title: Where AXTI sits against Sumitomo Electric, Freiberger, Wafer Technology, and broader substrate peers
chapters.body:
## A Thin-Filed Oligopoly

Compound semiconductor substrates occupy a narrow but load-bearing position in the photonics supply chain. The global market for InP, GaAs, and Ge single-crystal wafers is served by perhaps a dozen serious producers worldwide, with no more than three or four commanding meaningful share in any given material. AXT sits inside that oligopoly as the only pure-play compound substrate company listed on a US exchange, a structural singularity that shapes both its competitive leverage and its geopolitical exposure. Understanding where AXT wins, where it concedes ground, and why its Chinese-domiciled manufacturing is simultaneously its deepest cost advantage and its most contested risk requires mapping the field peer by peer.

## InP: A Three-Tier Competitive Map

The indium phosphide substrate market is effectively a three-tier structure. At the top sits **Sumitomo Electric Industries**, the Japanese conglomerate that operates one of the largest captive InP crystal-growth operations in the world alongside its own laser diode and fiber-optic device businesses. Sumitomo's vertical integration runs from InP substrate to compound epitaxial wafer to finished transceiver component, giving it both internal demand pull and the ability to sell substrates externally. That dual role — supplier to the same device makers it competes against downstream — creates a recurring customer-conflict dynamic that AXT, as a pure substrate company, does not face. Sumitomo's InP substrate business is embedded within a ¥4-trillion-revenue diversified industrial group, insulating it from the quarterly demand volatility that AXT must absorb directly on its income statement.

**Wafer Technology** (UK), now operating under IQE's broader compound wafer ecosystem following IQE's phased investment, represents the second tier: a smaller, technically capable European producer serving primarily the photonics and quantum research communities. Wafer Technology carries credibility in the 2-inch and 3-inch specialty market but has not demonstrated the capacity footprint to participate meaningfully in the 800G-era volume ramps that hyperscaler transceiver supply chains require. Its geographic position — UK-based, EU-adjacent, outside the Chinese export-control perimeter — gives it regulatory simplicity but limits raw-material integration advantages.

**JX Nippon Mining & Metals** (Japan), a subsidiary of ENEOS Holdings, maintains an InP substrate line as part of a broader high-purity metals and compound semiconductor franchise that includes GaAs and other III-V materials. JX Nippon is technically credible and well-capitalized, but InP substrates are a secondary business line within a group whose primary revenue comes from copper smelting and refining at a scale orders of magnitude larger. That context tends to produce conservative capacity-expansion behavior when the substrate market cycles upward — exactly the dynamic AXTI flagged when describing InP supply tightness through 2024-2025.

AXT's position in InP is defined less by volume leadership than by cost structure and wafer-size migration timing. Beijing Tongmei's manufacturing base in China gives AXT access to lower labor costs, proximity to upstream gallium and arsenic raw materials produced by its own subsidiaries (Baoding Tongmei, Nanjing Jinmei), and a capital expenditure environment shaped by Chinese policy support for domestic compound semiconductor manufacturing. The company has been among the most vocal about the 4-inch-to-6-inch InP wafer transition, with Morris Young repeatedly emphasizing on earnings calls that larger-format substrates reduce die-level cost for customers and align with the high-volume EML and DFB laser die economics demanded by 800G and 1.6T transceiver programs.

## GaAs: Freiberger's European Fortress

The gallium arsenide substrate market is older, larger, and more fragmented than InP. **Freiberger Compound Materials** (Germany) is the dominant independent GaAs substrate supplier in the Western world, holding particular strength in semi-insulating GaAs for RF power amplifiers and in the high-specification HBT substrates that Qorvo and MACOM use for 5G front-end modules. Freiberger is privately held, limiting visibility into its financials, but its customer relationships with the major RF foundries are long-standing and its German manufacturing base has proven resilient through multiple industry cycles. Freiberger competes for the same VCSEL and RF substrate accounts that AXT pursues, and the two companies represent the principal choices for Western device makers seeking to diversify away from Japanese or Chinese-domiciled supply.

Sumitomo Electric is also present in GaAs substrates, again benefiting from captive internal demand through its device manufacturing. **China Crystal Technologies** and several state-backed Chinese substrate producers have expanded GaAs capacity aggressively through the 2020s, supported by domestic demand from Chinese 5G infrastructure buildout and the broader Beijing policy push toward compound semiconductor self-sufficiency. These Chinese producers — less visible in Western trade publications but increasingly consequential in volume terms — compete primarily for Chinese domestic device-maker accounts rather than for the Lumentum or Coherent-type customer relationships that AXT addresses through Tongmei.

AXT's GaAs competitive position is strongest in the VCSEL substrate segment, where the combination of semi-insulating substrate quality, 6-inch-format capability, and established qualification at the major VCSEL fabs (Lumentum, Coherent, ams OSRAM supply chains) creates switching-cost protection. The Apple Face ID supply chain — which requires VCSEL epi-wafers grown on high-uniformity GaAs substrates — is a recurring reference point in AXT's investor communications, though AXT does not name Apple directly as a customer. GaAs substrate qualification cycles at Tier 1 VCSEL fabs typically run 12 to 24 months, a timeline that creates durable backlog visibility once a supplier is qualified and effectively prices out unqualified entrants during demand spikes.

## Germanium: Umicore's Domain

In germanium substrates, AXT competes primarily against **Umicore** (Belgium), the diversified materials technology group whose Electro-Optic Materials division controls significant Ge substrate capacity for multi-junction solar cell applications. Umicore's Ge substrate business is embedded within a €4-billion-revenue materials group with substantial recycling and battery materials operations, giving it capital resilience that a pure-play like AXT cannot match. AXT's Ge substrate revenue has historically been smaller than its InP and GaAs lines, and the multi-junction solar cell market — the primary Ge substrate end market — has followed a long secular trajectory shaped by satellite solar panel demand and terrestrial concentrator photovoltaic programs.

| Material | Primary Western Peers | AXT's Structural Advantage | AXT's Structural Disadvantage |
|---|---|---|---|
| InP | Sumitomo Electric, Wafer Technology, JX Nippon | Raw-material vertical integration; lower manufacturing cost base; 6-inch wafer transition timing | Smaller balance sheet; China geopolitical exposure |
| GaAs | Freiberger, Sumitomo Electric | VCSEL qualification depth; Chinese manufacturing cost structure | Freiberger's RF substrate relationship depth with Western foundries |
| Ge | Umicore, PPM Pure Metals | Vertical integration into Ge raw materials via Chinese subsidiaries | Umicore's capital base and established space-solar customer relationships |

## China's Export-Control Realignment

The August 2023 Chinese government export controls on gallium and germanium — and subsequent enforcement tightening through 2024 — created a structurally ambiguous environment for AXT. As a US-listed company with principal manufacturing in China, AXT sits at the intersection of two conflicting regulatory vectors. The controls restrict the export of raw gallium and germanium from China, potentially limiting AXT's ability to supply non-Chinese customers from Tongmei without navigating Chinese export licensing. At the same time, the controls elevate the strategic importance of domestically domiciled compound semiconductor supply chains within China, reinforcing AXT-Tongmei's positioning for Chinese optical module and device-maker accounts.

Chinese domestic competitors — including producers in Yunnan province benefiting from proximity to China's dominant gallium production base and state-directed capacity investment — have accelerated substrate output under this policy regime. These producers are less likely to pursue Western OEM qualifications in the near term but increasingly compete for the Chinese optical transceiver supply chain that feeds hyperscaler data center builds in China. AXT's competitive response to this pressure runs through the Tongmei STAR Market IPO thesis: a Shanghai-listed Tongmei subsidiary would raise RMB-denominated capital for capacity expansion, strengthen the company's positioning within China's semiconductor policy framework, and provide a local market anchor that purely foreign-owned substrate suppliers cannot replicate.

## The VGF Moat and Qualification Lock-In

Across all three substrate families, AXT's most durable competitive differentiator is the **Vertical Gradient Freeze** crystal-growth process developed under Morris Young's technical leadership from the company's earliest years. VGF produces lower dislocation-density crystals than the competing Liquid Encapsulated Czochralski (LEC) method that older substrate producers historically employed, and that crystal quality directly translates into higher laser diode yield for epi-wafer and device customers. The process know-how embedded in Tongmei's Beijing facilities — the specific furnace configurations, thermal-gradient protocols, and crucible chemistry using AXT's proprietary pyrolytic boron nitride (pBN) crucibles manufactured by its own subsidiary — is neither easily replicated nor quickly licensed. Combined with the 12-to-24-month customer qualification cycles that govern substrate sourcing decisions at laser diode and VCSEL fabs, VGF creates a moat that operates independently of pricing or balance sheet size.

For the 800G and 1.6T InP substrate cycle, this moat is most consequential. Transceiver makers running EML or DFB laser lines at volume cannot swap substrate suppliers between production runs without triggering yield-verification protocols that cost time and engineering resources neither side can afford during a demand upswing. AXT's long-standing qualifications at Coherent, Lumentum, and the major Japanese photonics houses mean that the incremental substrate demand from every additional 800G lane shipped accrues preferentially to already-qualified vendors — of which AXT, by scale and geography, is among the shortest list.

chapters.title: Timeline from 1986 founding through Tongmei migration, export controls, and the 800G/1.6T inflection
chapters.body:
## American Xtal Technology, 1986–2001: Fremont Origins and the Vertical-Integration Bet

Dr. Morris S. Young founded American Xtal Technology in Fremont, California in 1986 with a thesis that would define the company for four decades: that the most defensible position in compound semiconductor substrates was not simply growing crystals, but controlling the entire materials chain from high-purity gallium and arsenic upstream through finished wafer output. The company — later renamed AXT, Inc. and listed on NASDAQ as AXTI — built its early reputation supplying gallium arsenide semi-insulating substrates to the defence and telecom markets, a period when GaAs was still the workhorse of high-frequency electronics and optical fibre was only beginning its long march into carrier infrastructure.

The 1998 NASDAQ IPO gave AXT access to public capital at a moment when the telecommunications investment boom was at full pressure. The company used the capital to expand substrate capacity and extend its product range into indium phosphide — the material that would ultimately define its competitive position in the 2020s — as demand from DFB and EML laser diode makers began its first sustained growth cycle on the back of DWDM deployments. When the telecom bubble burst in 2001, AXT was exposed to the full severity of the correction, but Young used the downturn to accelerate a strategic pivot that would prove more consequential than any single product cycle.

## The Beijing Tongmei Migration, 2003–2015

Through the mid-2000s and into the 2010s, AXT systematically migrated its principal manufacturing operations from Fremont to its Beijing Tongmei subsidiary. The move reflected both cost-structure reality and a deeper logic: China was also home to the world's dominant reserves of gallium and germanium, and positioning manufacturing adjacent to raw-material supply in a single integrated flow would structurally lower input costs and give AXT supply-chain visibility that Western-only competitors could not replicate.

The company built out a network of upstream raw-material subsidiaries alongside Tongmei: Baoding Tongmei and Nanjing Jinmei for high-purity gallium and arsenic, JinMei and Chaoyang Tongmei for germanium and related inputs, and internal pyrolytic boron nitride (pBN) crucible production for the Bridgman-Stockbarger and vertical gradient freeze crystal-growth processes. By the time the migration was substantially complete, AXT had achieved a degree of upstream integration unusual in the substrate industry — the company could source, purify, crystal-grow, slice, and polish across a single Chinese manufacturing cluster, with Fremont retained as the US corporate headquarters and customer-facing interface.

This architecture carried latent geopolitical risk that was not yet visible in the 2010s commodity cycle. It would become the central tension of the company's narrative a decade later.

## Tongmei STAR Market IPO: A Multi-Year Pursuit

In 2021, AXT filed for a listing of the Beijing Tongmei subsidiary on the STAR Market of the Shanghai Stock Exchange — China's technology-focused exchange, modelled loosely on NASDAQ, that had launched in 2019. The rationale was straightforward: Tongmei, as the principal operating entity and manufacturing hub, represented the bulk of AXT's asset base, and a STAR Market listing would unlock a valuation that the NASDAQ parent — discounted by investors uncomfortable with China-domiciled operations — had never fully reflected. The capital raised would fund capacity expansion precisely when InP substrate demand was beginning its 800G-driven acceleration.

The approval process proved protracted. The China Securities Regulatory Commission and the Shanghai Stock Exchange put Tongmei through multiple rounds of regulatory inquiry across 2022, 2023, and into 2024, scrutinising everything from Tongmei's related-party arrangements with its NASDAQ parent to the export-control exposure of its raw-material subsidiaries. Each review cycle reset investor expectations and added uncertainty to AXT's capital-allocation timeline. By mid-2025, the Tongmei STAR Market listing remained the single largest unresolved value-unlock event on AXT's corporate calendar — a binary catalyst that had been pending long enough to generate scepticism among US investors about whether it would ever close.

## The August 2023 Export Controls: A Double-Edged Shock

On 4 August 2023, China's Ministry of Commerce announced that gallium and germanium products — the two raw materials at the core of AXT's upstream vertical integration — would require export licences effective immediately. The policy was framed as a reciprocal measure following successive rounds of US semiconductor export controls targeting advanced chips and equipment destined for China. For the compound semiconductor supply chain, the announcement triggered a global scramble: gallium is essential for GaAs and GaN substrates; germanium is essential for multi-junction solar cells and certain infrared applications.

The controls cut both ways for AXT. On one reading, they introduced regulatory friction into the company's ability to export substrates and raw materials from its Chinese subsidiaries to customers outside China — a source of operational uncertainty that weighed on near-term revenue visibility. On another reading, they reinforced the strategic moat: AXT was already China-domiciled and vertically integrated upstream, insulating it from the spot-market disruption that would afflict competitors dependent on Chinese gallium and germanium purchases. Western compound semiconductor substrate makers without equivalent upstream integration faced structurally higher input costs and supply uncertainty in the post-August-2023 world.

Young addressed the controls directly on earnings calls through late 2023 and 2024, characterising AXT's internal raw-material loop as a buffer against the regime's most disruptive effects while acknowledging that export licensing added procedural complexity to any cross-border material movement.

## The 800G Inflection and InP's New Gravity

The demand recovery that began in late 2023 and accelerated through 2024 was driven primarily by InP — not GaAs. The hyperscaler build-out of 800G data-centre interconnects required DFB, EML, and tunable laser diodes fabricated on InP substrates, and the ramp came faster than the substrate supply chain had prepared for. AXT, as one of the few vertically integrated InP substrate suppliers with meaningful production scale, was positioned at the centre of the bottleneck.

The 6-inch InP wafer transition became the defining technical milestone of the inflection. Moving from 4-inch to 6-inch substrates increases the usable die area per crystal growth run by roughly 125 percent, compressing unit substrate costs and enabling device makers to scale laser diode production without proportional increases in wafer throughput. AXT's progress on 6-inch InP qualification — with Tongmei's Bridgman growth capability at the centre of the development programme — emerged as the primary supply-side variable that customers and investors tracked through 2024 and 2025.

## Co-Packaged Optics and the 1.6T Forward Catalyst

The 1.6T pluggable transceiver ramp, beginning in earnest in 2025, extended the InP demand thesis. But the longer-duration catalyst was co-packaged optics: the CPO architecture, which integrates optical transceivers directly into switch-chip packages to eliminate the pluggable module altogether, requires external light source modules built on InP laser diodes. As hyperscalers began validating CPO platforms for next-generation AI cluster interconnects, InP substrate volumes per rack unit were set to increase materially relative to the pluggable era.

For a company that had spent four decades building the vertical integration infrastructure to supply InP at scale, the CPO inflection represented the demand cycle that the entire Tongmei manufacturing migration had unknowingly been preparing for. The open question entering 2026 was whether Tongmei's STAR Market listing — and the capital it would release — would arrive in time to fund the capacity expansion the cycle demanded.

chapters.title: VGF crystal growth, raw-material processing, substrate quality IP
chapters.body:
## The VGF Distinction

AXT's competitive foundation rests on a single technical decision made before the company existed. Morris Young, working as a researcher at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in the early 1980s, recognised that the dominant Liquid Encapsulated Czochralski (LEC) method for growing compound semiconductor crystals imposed thermal stresses that seeded dislocation networks throughout the boule — defects that propagated to every substrate sliced from it. His answer was Vertical Gradient Freeze: a sealed, pressurized ampoule in which a compound semiconductor melt solidifies from the bottom upward through a precisely controlled, shallow axial temperature gradient rather than being pulled through a volatile, high-temperature surface. Young brought the technique to commercialisation when he co-founded American Xtal Technology in 1986, and the process has been the firm's core proprietary asset ever since.

The physics of VGF delivers a structurally lower etch pit density (EPD) — the standard industry metric for threading dislocation density at the wafer surface — than LEC-grown material. In GaAs, LEC routinely yields EPD values above 10,000 cm⁻²; AXT's VGF process has driven semi-insulating GaAs EPD below 500 cm⁻² and, in premium lots, toward the low hundreds. In indium phosphide, where the compound's volatility and lower melting point make thermal management even more consequential, VGF confers a comparable advantage. Lower EPD reduces non-radiative recombination at active regions in laser diodes and VCSELs, which translates directly to device threshold current, wall-plug efficiency, and long-term reliability — parameters that matter acutely when a datacenter operator is qualifying a 800G CWDM8 transceiver array expected to run for seven years without maintenance.

The sealed-ampoule architecture also suppresses arsenic and phosphorus vapour loss during growth, a persistent quality-control challenge in open-crucible LEC that can alter stoichiometry and introduce point defects. AXT has refined its ampoule sealing, pressure management, and gradient-profile algorithms over four decades of cumulative production learning — a body of process knowledge that is largely embodied in engineering practice rather than in a bounded set of patent claims.

## Vertical Integration and the Crucible Advantage

The VGF furnace is only as good as the crucible that contains the melt. Pyrolytic boron nitride (pBN) — synthesised by chemical vapour deposition at high temperature to produce a layered hexagonal lattice — is the material of choice because it is chemically inert to gallium arsenide and indium phosphide melts, thermally stable above the growth temperatures involved, and machinable to the tight dimensional tolerances that determine thermal symmetry inside the ampoule. AXT manufactures pBN crucibles in-house through one of its Chinese subsidiaries rather than sourcing from third-party suppliers. That decision converts what would otherwise be a commodity procurement line item into a process-controlled input where dimensional consistency, surface finish, and purity are managed against AXT's own specifications rather than a vendor's catalogue.

Upstream of the crucible, AXT's four raw-material subsidiaries in China — Baoding Tongmei (gallium), Nanjing Jinmei (germanium), JinMei (gallium), and Chaoyang Tongmei (arsenic) — produce the high-purity starting materials that feed the Beijing Tongmei crystal-growth operation. Gallium metal for GaAs and InP synthesis is refined to 7N (99.99999%) purity; arsenic and phosphorus sources are processed to comparable specifications. Germanium is refined for Ge substrate production serving multi-junction space solar cells and infrared optics. This vertical integration was a deliberate strategic choice: sourcing 6N or 7N gallium on the open market in sufficient volumes, at consistent quality, is difficult and expensive. By controlling refining capacity in-house, AXT can tune the impurity profile of its starting material to the specific requirements of each crystal-growth programme — a variable that affects both EPD and electrical uniformity in ways that external purity specifications alone cannot capture.

The 2023 Chinese gallium and germanium export controls introduced a regulatory dimension to this integrated supply position. AXT's raw-material subsidiaries operate within China's licensing framework; export of refined gallium and germanium from China now requires government approval under rules introduced in August 2023 and tightened through 2024. For AXT the controls cut in two directions: they complicated the logistics of raw-material export for external customers while simultaneously underscoring the strategic value of AXT's Chinese-domiciled, vertically integrated supply chain for customers who need compliant substrate supply.

## EPD Engineering and the Six-Inch Transition

As the datacenter transceiver market migrated from 100G to 400G and then toward 800G and 1.6T line rates, substrate quality requirements tightened. Higher-speed EML (electro-absorption modulated laser) and DFB laser devices are more sensitive to dislocation-induced active-region defects because device dimensions have shrunk and the tolerable threshold-current spread across a wafer has narrowed. AXT has invested in EPD reduction programmes that combine refined gradient profiles, tighter thermal uniformity specifications across the boule diameter, and enhanced post-growth annealing steps.

The simultaneous push to larger wafer diameters — 4-inch and 6-inch InP — creates a yield engineering challenge that is fundamentally a thermal problem. Larger diameter means larger radial temperature gradients during solidification, which seeds more dislocations unless the furnace geometry and gradient-control algorithm are redesigned for the new form factor. AXT has worked through this transition on GaAs (4-inch and 6-inch SI and SC wafers are in production) and has been scaling 4-inch InP toward 6-inch, where the economics of co-packaged optics (CPO) external light source module production depend on wafer-level throughput. Thermal uniformity across a 6-inch InP boule, and the translation of that uniformity to low EPD and consistent electrical properties across the full substrate area, is the central yield-engineering problem the company was actively prosecuting through the 2024-2026 window.

## Patents, Trade Secrets, and the Moat Architecture

AXT's patent portfolio covers aspects of VGF furnace design, ampoule geometry, gradient-control systems, and pBN crucible fabrication methods. As a company with fewer than 600 employees and principal operations in China, it does not publish a detailed patent count in its SEC filings, and the portfolio is modest in volume relative to larger semiconductor manufacturers. The more consequential IP layer is trade secret: the specific gradient profiles for each crystal composition and diameter, the furnace thermal models calibrated over decades of production data, the ampoule sealing and pressure recipes, and the yield-prediction models that link growth parameters to EPD outcomes. These are resident in the engineering organisation and in the institutional memory of a technical workforce that has, in several cases, been with the Beijing Tongmei operation for fifteen or more years.

That tenure concentration is itself a strategic consideration. The depth of process knowledge embedded in AXT's Beijing team is not easily replicated from first principles, and the combination of controlled raw-material supply, in-house pBN crucible manufacturing, and accumulated VGF process refinement represents a barrier that a new entrant would require years — and a willingness to operate at a loss through the learning curve — to match. The Tongmei STAR Market IPO process, if completed, would make some of that institutional knowledge more legible to external investors, but the process moat itself would remain proprietary.

chapters.title: China geopolitical exposure, Tongmei IPO timing, customer concentration, ASP volatility, scale, competitive
chapters.body:
## China Geopolitical Exposure: A US Company with Its Factory Inside the Wire

The structural tension at the centre of every AXT investment thesis was the same one that defined its corporate architecture: the company was incorporated in Fremont, California, listed on the NASDAQ, and reported in US dollars, yet its principal manufacturing asset — Beijing Tongmei Xtal Technology — sat inside the People's Republic of China. That arrangement had been deliberate. Morris Young migrated substrate crystal-growing operations to Beijing over the course of the 2000s and 2010s, chasing lower labour costs, proximity to raw-material supply chains, and access to China's expanding compound-semiconductor ecosystem. By the mid-2020s, Tongmei was not merely an offshore manufacturing site but the operational core of the business, supported by a cluster of upstream subsidiaries — Baoding Tongmei, Nanjing Jinmei, JinMei, and Chaoyang Tongmei — that produced the high-purity gallium, arsenic, germanium, and pyrolytic boron nitride crucibles that fed the crystal-growth furnaces.

That vertical integration gave AXT genuine cost and supply-chain advantages, but it also meant that its productive capacity was subject to Chinese regulatory jurisdiction, export-licensing authority, and the escalating cadence of US-China technology friction. Beijing's August 2023 export controls on gallium and germanium imposed licensing requirements on outbound shipments of raw materials that AXT's subsidiaries both produced and consumed. The controls cut in two directions simultaneously: they constrained the ability of AXT's Chinese entities to ship freely to non-Chinese customers, while simultaneously reinforcing the competitive moat of Chinese-domiciled compound semiconductor supply chains against foreign competitors who sourced gallium and germanium on open markets. For AXT, which processed gallium and germanium internally before it ever left its own facilities, the net effect was ambiguous — a structural benefit to the Chinese subsidiary's competitive position paired with a persistent cloud over the legal and licensing environment governing international substrate shipments.

Broader geopolitical risk ran deeper than any single export-control regime. A significant escalation in US-China trade restrictions — whether through expanded entity-list designations, foreign direct product rules applied to compound semiconductor substrates, or forced divestiture requirements of the kind that had reshaped other dual-listed China-operating companies — could impair AXT's ability to operate Tongmei, repatriate capital, or maintain its customer base in the United States and Japan.

## The Tongmei IPO Waiting Room

From 2021 onward, AXT management presented the Tongmei STAR Market Shanghai IPO as a value-unlock catalyst — a path to listing Beijing Tongmei as a standalone entity on China's technology-focused exchange, monetising a minority stake, raising capital for capacity expansion, and crystallising the subsidiary's valuation independently of AXT's NASDAQ multiple. The logic was straightforward. Tongmei, as a vertically integrated Chinese compound semiconductor substrate manufacturer with government-aligned positioning in the gallium and germanium strategic-material supply chain, could plausibly command a richer domestic Chinese technology-sector multiple than the consolidated AXT entity attracted from US small-cap investors.

The execution proved considerably more complicated. Multiple regulatory review cycles ran through 2023, 2024, and into 2025 without a completed listing. China Securities Regulatory Commission review processes for STAR Market candidates were not fast under the best of circumstances, and AXT's cross-border corporate structure — a US-listed parent retaining a controlling interest in a PRC operating entity — introduced layers of regulatory scrutiny that pure-play domestic candidates did not face. Each delay extended the window of uncertainty on AXT's balance sheet: the capital that a successful Tongmei offering would have provided for additional furnace capacity and 6-inch wafer infrastructure remained hypothetical.

The IPO uncertainty was also a second-order constraint on visibility into Tongmei's standalone financial profile. Because Tongmei had not achieved independent listing status, its financial disclosures remained consolidated within AXT's SEC filings rather than subject to the granular segment reporting that a separately listed entity would have generated. Investors, analysts, and customers attempting to assess Tongmei's standalone revenue mix, margin structure, and capacity trajectory were working from aggregated AXT disclosures rather than primary Tongmei financial statements.

## Customer Concentration and Visibility

AXT's compound semiconductor substrate revenue was concentrated in a relatively small number of device manufacturers, each of which was itself subject to the upstream demand volatility of its own end markets. The principal InP customer set included compound epitaxial-wafer producers such as IQE, vertically integrated photonics manufacturers such as Coherent and Lumentum, and the Japanese photonics ecosystem — Mitsubishi Electric, Sharp, Sony — that had historically anchored Asian optical-component supply chains. GaAs substrate demand was similarly concentrated, with VCSEL manufacturers (Lumentum, Coherent, ams OSRAM) and RF power device makers (Qorvo, MACOM) representing the primary pull.

The consequence of that concentration was that a single customer's inventory digestion cycle, a programme cancellation, or a sourcing-strategy shift could produce an outsized swing in AXT's quarterly revenue. The 3D sensing cycle that had driven GaAs substrate demand through the iPhone Face ID era illustrated the dynamic: when Apple's supply chain built inventory ahead of a major handset cycle, AXT's GaAs business swelled; when that same supply chain digested accumulated stock, the drawdown was abrupt. The 800G/1.6T transceiver inflection created a structurally similar visibility challenge in InP — hyperscaler capital expenditure pulled forward demand, but the translation from hyperscaler purchase-order commitments at the optical module level to substrate pull at AXT's furnaces ran through multiple intermediary layers, each of which could buffer or amplify the demand signal.

## Substrate ASP Volatility Through the Cycle

Substrate pricing for InP, GaAs, and germanium was not set in deep liquid commodity markets. Average selling prices reflected negotiated terms between a small number of substrate suppliers and a small number of device manufacturers, with pricing shaped by capacity utilisation, new competitive entrants, wafer-diameter transitions, and the balance of supply and demand at each node of the compound semiconductor value chain. Historically, AXT's revenue oscillated within a $60–110 million annual range, a band that reflected both volume variability and ASP swings across cycles.

The 6-inch InP wafer transition that was underway in the mid-2020s introduced a specific ASP tension. Larger-diameter substrates commanded higher per-wafer prices but also required capital investment in furnace and processing equipment scaled for the new geometry. If the transition accelerated faster than Tongmei's capacity expansion, AXT could face a period of supply constraint during which customers hedged by qualifying alternative suppliers — permanently eroding the incumbent share that had been built over years of qualification cycles. If the transition moved more slowly than capital expenditure on furnace expansion implied, fixed-cost absorption would pressure margins.

## Small-Cap Scale Constraints

With annual revenue in the $60–110 million historical range, AXT operated at a scale that imposed structural disadvantages relative to diversified compound semiconductor and photonics groups. Research and development spending was constrained by revenue size; the ability to absorb a failed product generation or a delayed customer qualification without material financial impact was limited; access to capital markets for equity financing was conditioned on the sentiment of a small-cap investor base that was sensitive to quarterly earnings misses and IPO milestone slippage. Management bandwidth — with Morris Young as founder, chairman, president, and chief executive officer across four decades — concentrated strategic decision-making in a founder-led structure that was both an organisational strength and a succession-risk concentration point.

## Competitive Intensity: Sumitomo, Freiberger, and the Domestic Chinese Ecosystem

The competitive landscape for compound semiconductor substrates was neither fragmented nor monopolistic — it was oligopolistic, with a small number of technically capable suppliers competing on qualification history, wafer-geometry capability, and delivered quality rather than price alone. Sumitomo Electric Industries retained a strong position in both InP and GaAs substrates, backed by deep vertical integration and the technical credibility of a major Japanese industrial group. Freiberger Compound Materials of Germany was the principal European GaAs substrate supplier, with comparable quality credentials and customer relationships running back decades into the III-V device industry.

The August 2023 China gallium and germanium export controls created a new competitive dynamic by improving the relative position of Chinese-domiciled substrate producers — including Tongmei itself — at the expense of foreign substrate suppliers who sourced gallium and germanium on international markets. Yet that same policy environment also created space for other Chinese compound semiconductor substrate entrants to invest in domestic production capacity, potentially intensifying competition within China for the substrate customers that Tongmei was simultaneously trying to serve and grow. AXT's competitive moat was real — built on decades of Czochralski and vertical gradient freeze crystal-growth expertise and long-standing customer qualifications — but it was not impregnable in an environment where Chinese industrial policy explicitly incentivised domestic compound semiconductor self-sufficiency at every level of the stack.

chapters.title: InP 800G/1.6T scaling, CPO ELS substrate demand, Tongmei IPO unlock, 2026-2030 horizon
chapters.body:
## The Convergence Point

By the spring of 2026, AXT, Inc. stood at an unusually compressed intersection of demand cycles. The 800G pluggable transceiver ramp that had begun pulling hard on indium phosphide substrates through 2024 was accelerating rather than plateauing, with hyperscaler capital expenditure programs for AI data-centre buildout sustaining wafer orders that earlier analyst models had expected to moderate. The 1.6T generation was transitioning from qualification to early production. Co-packaged optics architectures, which had been a speculative thesis two years prior, were beginning to extract tangible substrate volume commitments from the module ecosystem. The Tongmei STAR Market IPO, long suspended in regulatory review, remained unresolved but structurally consequential. And the China gallium and germanium export-control regime, introduced in August 2023, was reshaping the competitive landscape in ways that cut differently for a US-listed company whose principal manufacturing operations were Chinese-domiciled. Taken together, these vectors defined a strategic posture that AXT's founder Morris Young had not navigated before in quite this configuration.

## InP Substrate at the 800G/1.6T Inflection

Indium phosphide substrates underpin the laser diode and electroabsorption modulated laser (EML) devices that sit inside every high-speed optical transceiver. At 800G per port — the generation that hyperscalers began deploying in earnest across AI cluster interconnects in 2024 — the substrate intensity per transmitted bit roughly held constant, but the absolute volume of substrates required expanded sharply as installed port counts scaled. The shift to 1.6T, anticipated across 2026 and into 2027, compressed the per-bit economics further while requiring tighter substrate specification tolerances for the higher-modulation-format devices.

AXT's positioning in this demand curve reflected two durable structural advantages. First, the company had pursued the transition from two-inch and three-inch InP wafers toward four-inch and six-inch diameter formats for years before the 800G ramp arrived, meaning that the larger-area, lower-cost-per-device substrates needed for high-volume transceiver production were already in the product catalogue when module makers needed them. Second, vertical integration through the Chinese raw-material subsidiaries — Baoding Tongmei producing high-purity gallium, the Nanjing Jinmei and JinMei entities providing additional refined materials, and Chaoyang Tongmei supplying pyrolytic boron nitride crucibles for the Czochralski crystal-growth process — gave AXT a cost structure that pure-substrate competitors without upstream integration could not readily replicate.

Competitive framing for the InP substrate market placed Sumitomo Electric as the principal Japanese incumbent and Wafer Technology (UK) as a smaller alternative source, with the Chinese-domiciled supply chain inside Beijing Tongmei representing AXT's primary manufacturing engine. At the six-inch diameter node, the production learning curve was steeper, yield management more demanding, and the number of qualified suppliers globally remained narrow — a structural constraint that advantaged incumbents already in customer qualifications.

## CPO and the External Light Source Imperative

The co-packaged optics architecture, which routes optical I/O directly onto switching silicon packages rather than through pluggable front-panel modules, introduced a demand vector that was genuinely incremental to the pluggable transceiver cycle rather than a replacement for it. CPO switches require an external light source module — a separate InP-based laser array supplying the continuous-wave optical power that the silicon photonics modulator then encodes with data. That external light source module, whether implemented as a multi-wavelength laser array or a bank of single-mode DFB lasers, consumes InP substrate that is additive to the substrate demand already flowing through the pluggable transceiver supply chain.

The scale of that incremental demand remained a subject of range-wide disagreement among market participants as of the frozen snapshot. CPO deployment timelines had slipped repeatedly as switching-ASIC integration complexity proved harder to resolve than roadmaps suggested; at the same time, the architectural pressure from power-consumption constraints at the AI cluster scale was inexorable, and hyperscaler procurement teams were working through CPO qualifications in parallel with continued pluggable 800G and 1.6T deployments. For AXT, the CPO thesis represented a call option on substrate volume beyond the pluggable cycle — not yet fully exercised, but structurally underwritten by the InP dependency of any CPO external light source design.

## GaAs and Germanium: The Secondary Cycles

Beyond InP, AXT's two remaining principal substrate families — gallium arsenide and germanium — each carried their own demand dynamics through the 2026-2030 window.

GaAs semi-insulating substrates supporting VCSEL production had navigated a demand trough in 2023 and early 2024 as the smartphone 3D-sensing upgrade cycle moderated and handset unit volumes recovered slowly. The underlying franchise remained intact: Apple's Face ID supply chain continued to consume VCSEL substrates for biometric sensing; automotive LiDAR design wins at Tier 1 suppliers were pulling GaAs VCSEL content into vehicles at volumes that grew slowly but compounded over multi-year platform cycles; and datacom VCSEL applications for short-reach 850-nm links inside data centres provided a third demand leg. RF power GaAs, serving 5G base-station power amplifier content at Qorvo, MACOM, and their peers, tracked macro wireless capital expenditure cycles that were mid-cycle as of 2026, with 6G standardisation work beginning to define the next equipment generation.

Germanium substrates serving multi-junction solar cells for space applications — Spectrolab (Boeing), Azur Space, and the broader GEO/LEO satellite solar panel supply chain — represented a smaller but high-specification segment where AXT's Ge substrate production carried premium pricing relative to terrestrial solar applications. Satellite constellation buildout activity, particularly in low-earth-orbit programmes, was sustaining demand for space-qualified III-V solar cells and therefore for the Ge substrates beneath them.

## The Tongmei IPO Unlock

No strategic variable in AXT's 2026-2030 outlook carried more capital-structure significance than the resolution of the Beijing Tongmei STAR Market IPO process. The Tongmei subsidiary had been pursuing a listing on the Shanghai STAR Market — China's high-technology equity board — since 2021. Multiple regulatory review cycles with the China Securities Regulatory Commission and the Shanghai Stock Exchange had extended the process well past the initial anticipated timeline, reflecting both the general tightening of CSRC review standards across 2022 and 2023 and the specific complexity of a Chinese-operating subsidiary whose ultimate parent was a US-listed NASDAQ company.

A completed Tongmei IPO would achieve three simultaneous objectives. It would provide direct capital to Beijing Tongmei for capacity expansion — additional crystal-growth furnaces, larger-diameter InP and GaAs boule production, and six-inch InP yield improvement programmes. It would unlock public-market valuation for the Chinese operating entity on a separate from the AXTI consolidated multiple, potentially creating a sum-of-parts premium for shareholders who had been pricing the Tongmei asset through the compressed small-cap NASDAQ multiple. And it would demonstrate access to Chinese domestic capital markets for ongoing operational and expansion financing, reducing the dependence on AXT's US-level balance sheet to fund Chinese manufacturing investment.

The risk to this scenario was straightforward: continued CSRC processing delays, a shift in China's policy environment toward US-affiliated issuers on domestic exchanges, or a deterioration in the STAR Market valuation environment that reduced the economic rationale for the listing. Neither outcome could be excluded as of the frozen snapshot, but the directional pressure from AXT's management remained toward completion.

## China Export Controls: Structural Constraint and Competitive Repositioning

The August 2023 Chinese export controls on gallium and germanium — and the subsequent 2024 enforcement actions — inserted a geopolitical variable into AXT's operating model that interacted with the company's positioning in an asymmetric way. As a US-listed company with principal manufacturing inside China, AXT occupied an unusual middle position: subject to US export-control concerns from the American regulatory direction, while also operating within the Chinese-domiciled supply chain that the August 2023 controls were designed to protect and leverage.

The practical effect through 2024 and into 2025 was to raise raw-material procurement complexity and average selling price dynamics for gallium and germanium globally, benefiting AXT's vertically integrated cost position relative to substrate competitors who sourced gallium and germanium externally. Non-Chinese compound semiconductor substrate producers in Japan, Germany, and the UK faced higher input costs and supply-chain uncertainty that AXT, drawing on its own Chinese raw-material subsidiaries, did not face to the same degree.

The counter-risk was the export-restriction direction: to the extent that Chinese authorities moved to restrict gallium- or germanium-containing substrate exports — a scenario discussed in policy circles if not yet implemented — AXT's ability to serve non-Chinese customers from its Beijing Tongmei manufacturing base would face incremental friction. That scenario remained a tail risk rather than a base case through the frozen snapshot, but the scenario-planning burden it placed on AXT's customer relationships with Japanese, European, and North American device makers was real.

## The 2026-2030 Compound Photonics Cycle

The aggregate demand picture that AXT faced across the 2026-2030 planning horizon was more constructive than at any point in the company's history. The InP substrate franchise, which had operated for decades as a niche telecom-cycle-linked business with revenue in the tens of millions of dollars, was being repriced by the AI infrastructure buildout — a capex programme of a scale and duration that earlier optical market cycles had not produced. The CPO architecture added a second InP demand curve that was partially uncorrelated with the pluggable transceiver cycle. GaAs VCSEL demand carried durable consumer, automotive, and datacom legs. Germanium served a growing space-solar market.

Against that demand backdrop, the Tongmei IPO resolution and the China export-control policy trajectory were the principal binary variables. The former offered a capital structure catalyst; the latter defined the operational risk envelope for a company whose manufacturing base was structurally Chinese even as its customer relationships and equity listing were structurally American. Morris Young's task in the years through 2030 was to hold both dimensions simultaneously — converting the photonics demand inflection into substrate volume and margin, while managing the geopolitical configuration that had made AXT's vertical integration both a structural strength and a structural exposure.

## Appendix C — Financial Reference

AXT reports on a calendar fiscal year ending December 31. Historical revenue has ranged in the **$60–110 million USD** band across cycles, with profitability oscillating between modest positive and modest negative depending on substrate average selling prices and capacity utilization. Gross margin progression is the primary operating lever, driven by InP and GaAs ASPs, the share of 6-inch versus smaller-diameter production, and utilization at the Beijing Tongmei facility. Vertical integration into raw-material subsidiaries — Baoding Tongmei, Nanjing Jinmei, JinMei, and Chaoyang Tongmei — provides structural cost-of-goods advantage.
